  6. Put the revisions back in your project folder. If you have the document the PDF came from, have Claude revise that and make a new PDF. If you only have the PDF, ask it how it can make the changes before replacing anything. Once the revised files are saved and checked, it can delete the temporary download. This keeps your project folder tidy; it doesn't remove the copies in Adobe.

If you do this often, put the steps in a skill. Then you can use /adobe to open the PDF and say “read my notes” when you're done. Ask:

Make me a skill called /adobe. If I already have one, adapt it to this workflow.

When I run it, open the PDF I most recently mentioned or you most recently sent me in the Adobe widget. Or I might call /adobe file/path/here.pdf; in that case, open that file. Remind me to click "Show in another pane" to see it in a larger format.

When I say "read my notes" or "read my comments":
1. Find the copy I saved with comments.
2. Compare its file size with the original, and check that the comments are actually present.
3. Download the version with comments. If Adobe doesn't give you a download link, use the compression step, then check that the downloaded file still contains the comments.
4. Extract the PDF's saved annotations, not just its page text. Read each comment with its page number and the passage it refers to. Address the comments in the editable source document, if we have it, then regenerate the PDF in our project folder. If we only have a PDF, explain how you can edit it and agree the approach with me before replacing the original. Tell me about any comments you couldn't address.
5. Once the revised source and PDF are saved and checked, delete the temporary local download with comments. If we edited only the PDF, check that revised PDF before deleting the download.

Alternatively, split this into two skills. /adobe-in or /adobe-annotate could upload your local PDF to Adobe and open the widget beside your chat. Then /adobe-out or /adobe-revise could handle steps 1–5 in the prompt above, so you can invoke the skill instead of writing “address my comments” each time.

docs.title: Blattify — beta testing
docs.text:
You don't have to work through this site on your own. Blattify helps your AI agent figure out what you're already doing, suggest a useful next step, and walk you through it on a real task. It uses the essentials and the Master Checklist, so you can skip familiar practices and spend time on what would help.

This skill is in beta

We're testing how well it teaches these workflows in different projects and agent setups. Tell us what worked or where you got stuck.

docs.title: Install it in the agent you already use
docs.text:
Start with Claude or Codex on your computer. You don't need the starter kit or experience installing skills. Ask your agent:

Install the blattify skill from https://github.com/chrisblattman/claudeblattman/tree/main/skills/blattify in this app. Copy the whole folder, including SKILL.md and all its reference files. If I already have it, preserve my customizations and check for duplicate versions.

Tell me when it's ready and whether I need to start a new session to use it.

docs.title: Try it on your work
docs.text:
Once the skill is available, ask:

/blattify

The agent asks which projects to consider and where to keep your shared progress record. It looks at the practices you already use, recommends a useful improvement, and helps you try it. You can also ask for something narrower: “Use Blattify to help me prepare for project meetings.”

As you work, it explains the practice, shows you how to use it, and brings you into the decisions. It saves progress in the place you've chosen so you can return later and pick up where you left off.

You choose what to adopt. Blattify can guide you through installing another skill or connecting an app when needed; it doesn't require setting up everything on this site before you can begin.

Read the skill's instructions on GitHub.

docs.title: Switch to the desktop app
docs.text:
If you're still doing all your AI work in a terminal, switch to the desktop app. For the kind of work on this site, I'd treat it as essential. Being able to see what the agent made, point at what you want changed, and work in the same browser makes a huge difference to the back-and-forth.

Much of this is possible from a terminal too. What I prefer about the desktop apps is having the conversation, the work, and the controls together—and managing several sessions in one working window. It makes it easier to see what's happening, switch between tasks, and give useful feedback.

The rest of this page gives you a few things to try as you work. I prefer Codex's preview and feedback interface right now, but most of these habits work in both Claude and Codex. You don't need to learn every feature before getting started.

Current as of November 2026. App controls change; the linked guides have the latest details.

docs.title: 1. Manage multiple sessions in one working window
docs.text:
Keep several sessions going in one working window. Have one agent work on your slide deck while another investigates a question and a third revises a document. The sidebar keeps those conversations together: switch to the one that needs your attention, give it feedback, then return to another while it works. For me, this is one of the biggest conveniences of the desktop apps.

Rename your chats so they mean something to you. “Funder deck — revise opening” or “August trip — compare options” gives your brain a useful signpost when you return to the list. You can ask the agent to rename the chat.

Start a sub-task when part of the work deserves its own conversation. In Claude, a suggested task can open as a new session beneath the original in the sidebar. You might keep drafting a report in the main chat while a related conversation checks a source or explores another approach. That gives you somewhere to follow up on that piece of work separately.

Use a side chat for a quick question along the way. Claude's side chats let you ask something like “What does this term mean?” without interrupting the main task. The side discussion stays separate from the main conversation, so you can get your answer and return to the work.

Sort your sessions so the right work is easy to find. Grouping by day helps you pick up something you worked on recently. Pinning keeps the chats you return to often near the top, and project groups keep related work together. Use the arrangement that makes sense for your work.

docs.title: 2. Pick up the same session on another device
docs.text:
Being able to pick up the same work from any of my computers is a big advantage. I move between my laptop, my always-on computer at home, and my office desktop. With them connected, I can find and continue my sessions from whichever device I'm using. I don't have to remember which machine I was sitting at when I started.

Both Claude and Codex support this. Once you've enabled remote access and connected the relevant devices, the apps make it easy to find a session, check its progress, and continue the conversation. The work still runs on its host computer, so that machine needs to stay awake and online with the agent running. That's one reason an always-on home computer is useful: I can close my laptop while work continues there.

Help me connect my devices so I can find and continue my sessions from my other computers. Walk me through the setup, explain where the work will run, and tell me which computer needs to stay on.

Claude can also connect terminal sessions through Remote Control. The desktop advantage is having the sessions and their controls together in the app. See Claude's cross-device sessions and Codex's remote connections.

Cloud sessions: keep working when your computer is off

A cloud session runs on the provider's computers, so it can continue working even when your own computers are off. Remote access to your home computer still depends on that computer being on; a cloud session doesn't.

In the desktop app, choose a cloud environment when starting the task, instead of a local project. Ask the agent to help set up the files and tools the task needs there. Cloud sessions don't automatically have access to the folders or signed-in apps on your computer.

Both Claude and Codex can also start cloud tasks from the terminal. The convenience here is choosing where the task runs and checking its progress in the app. See Claude cloud sessions and Codex environments.

docs.title: 3. Open a webpage beside the conversation
docs.text:
If you're discussing a webpage, ask the agent to open it beside the chat. It could be a site you're reading, a dashboard you're building, or a draft you want to revise. Looking at the page while you discuss it makes the conversation much easier.

Open this page beside our conversation so we can look at it together.
Opening pages and local files

Both apps have a built-in browser. Click the link the agent gives you, or ask it to open the page. In Claude, keep local files in a folder connected to the project; a file link outside those folders may not open in the app.

See the Codex browser guide or Claude browser guide for the controls in your app.

docs.title: 4. See the document you're making
docs.text:
Ask to see the work. If the agent has made a slide deck, open the slides. If it has made a document, look at the document. You can give much better feedback when you're looking at the result: “This table is unreadable,” “The opening takes too long,” or “Put the funding request earlier.”

Open the draft so I can review it while we talk. If this app can't preview the file, help me open it in the right application.
What can each app preview?

Codex can preview documents, spreadsheets, presentations, and PDFs beside the chat. Claude can open PDFs and HTML in its browser pane and text files in its file pane. The available viewer depends on the file format.

See Codex file previews or Claude file panes.

docs.title: 5. Point at exactly what you want changed
docs.text:
In Codex's browser, select Annotate, click something or draw a rectangle around it, and leave a comment. “Drop this.” “Make this heading smaller.” “These two paragraphs belong together.” Add several comments, then send them back to the agent in one message.

You shouldn't need to learn the vocabulary of web design to say that a box is too big. It's also how we're editing this site. The browser comments guide shows the controls.

In my experience, Claude's feedback tools aren't quite as ubiquitous. You can leave several replies on its messages or a plan, and comment on changed lines in the Git changes view. But I haven't had the same annotation workflow for website or PDF previews. That's a downside for the way I work. I'd bet that gap will narrow as the apps develop.

Claude also has a separate Docs interface with comments; that is different from annotating a webpage or PDF preview.

In either app, give the agent the whole set of comments, let it make a pass, then look again. Go back and forth until you're happy with the result. The annotation guide shows how to leave comments in each app, including Google Docs and PDFs.

docs.title: 6. Keep an eye on the agent’s browser work
docs.text:
Connect Chrome and the agent can work in the browser you already use, including sites where you're signed in. It can read pages, follow links, click buttons, and fill in forms. Think about the university portal you keep putting off, or the five tabs you opened to compare conference venues.

Claude can control Chrome from the terminal too, and you can watch it work there. The desktop advantage is the workspace: keep the conversation and browser in view together, follow what the agent is doing, and give feedback as you go. The built-in browser is particularly convenient for this because the page sits beside the chat.

Start by asking it to help with the connection:

Help me connect Chrome so you can work in my open tabs. Do the setup you can, and walk me through anything I need to do myself.

Once connected, give it an ordinary task: “Compare the venues in these tabs against our dates, budget, and expected attendance. Put the options in a table in this project.”

For work in desktop applications, Codex on a Mac also offers a small picture-in-picture preview during Computer Use, so you can keep an eye on the app it's operating while you work elsewhere. This is a particular Computer Use feature, rather than a preview of every Chrome session; on Windows, Computer Use operates in the foreground. See the Computer Use guide.

How to connect Chrome

In Codex, go to Settings → Computer Use, install the Chrome extension, and use @Chrome in your request. In Claude, connect the Claude in Chrome extension. Use the Chrome profile where you're signed in to the sites you need.

The browser inside the app has its own login session; it doesn't automatically inherit your Chrome tabs. If you want the agent to work in your existing tabs, say so. For forms, tell it whether you want a draft or a submitted form.

See Codex's Chrome setup or Claude's Chrome setup.

docs.title: 7. Review changes in a pane
docs.text:
When the agent revises a text file, ask it to show you what changed. You can inspect changes in a terminal too; the desktop pane puts the added and removed lines beside the conversation and lets you attach feedback to them. This works for a Markdown document as well as an analysis script.

Try: “Show me the changes you made to this draft so I can review them.” Both apps have a changes view: Claude's diff view and Codex's review pane.

docs.title: 8. Manage your automations in one place
docs.text:
When you find yourself asking for the same thing every week, ask the agent to schedule it. Scheduling is possible from a terminal too. What makes the desktop apps useful is having your scheduled tasks and their results together in one place. For example:

Every Friday at 3 p.m., review this project's updates and prepare a brief for Monday: decisions made, open questions, and what needs my attention. Save it in this project folder.

Open the app's Scheduled section to find your automations, adjust their instructions or timing, and inspect previous runs. Open a run's conversation to ask follow-up questions or keep working on its result. Refine the instructions after the first run, just as you would for any other task.

What needs to stay running?

For scheduled work running on your computer, leave the app running and the machine awake and online. A task that needs your local files can't work on them while your laptop is asleep. Ask the agent to explain where your scheduled task runs and how to check its results.

See Codex scheduling or Claude scheduling.

docs.title: 9. Bring several folders into the same project
docs.text:
Your project might have drafts in Dropbox, data in a synced Box folder, and code in a local GitHub checkout. Add those folders to the project so the agent can work across them. The files can stay where they are. Terminal agents can use multiple folders too; the app gives you a convenient place to manage them.

Tell the agent where the material lives and ask it to help connect the folders. For example: “This project uses these three folders: [paths]. Help me make all three available in this session.”

Where to add folders

In Codex, use Edit project → Add folder. In Claude, add folders to the session or its saved environment. See Codex projects or Claude's folder instructions.

docs.title: Other features I've heard about but haven't yet tried
docs.text:
LaTeX editor. Codex has a local LaTeX editor and compiler with a PDF preview beside the conversation. It doesn't replace my Overleaf collaboration setup, but I'm excited to try the editing interface.

Record and replay. Demonstrate a recurring task on your computer and let the AI turn it into a reusable skill—for example, downloading a monthly report or filing an expense. OpenAI calls this Record & Replay, available on Mac. Claude has Record a skill in Cowork on Mac for Pro, Max, and Team users. Both create a skill you can review and refine, rather than simply replaying an identical series of clicks.

docs.title: Your first session
docs.text:
Pick something you actually want to get done. A family trip to plan, or a decision at work where the information is scattered across a dozen files. You’ll learn more by getting an answer that matters to you.

You don’t need to code or use a terminal. You do need to give the agent a runway: point it in the right direction, supply the information it needs, and keep correcting the course. The aim is to get the plane to take off and land.

docs.title: 1. Choose an agent
docs.text:
Start with Claude Code or Codex, OpenAI’s agent. If you already use one, keep it. If you already pay for Claude or ChatGPT, check what your plan includes before buying something else. You can add a second AI later.

For today, the useful decision is which app you’ll open and use.

Why Claude Blattman switched to Codex — November 2026

I started with Claude and now use Codex as my main workspace, including to coordinate other AIs. Read why I switched to Codex, and why my preference could change again.

I’ve chosen an agent.

docs.title: 2. Install the app
docs.text:
Use the official Claude download page or OpenAI desktop guide. Download the version for your computer, install it, and sign in.

In Claude, open the Code tab. In OpenAI’s desktop app, select Codex if the app opens in ChatGPT. You want the part of the app that can work with a folder on your computer.

I’ve installed the app and opened its agent workspace.

docs.title: 3. Set permissions
docs.text:
Permissions control what the agent can read or change and when it asks you first. Claude and Codex offer similar choices, though the names and boundaries differ. Ask:

Help me understand the permissions for this session. What can you read and change, and which actions will ask me first? Walk me through the controls in this app. I want to work in my project folder and keep important decisions with me.
What do the permission modes mean?

Use the permissions control below the message box. Here’s the short version; available options can vary by version and organization.

Claude Code Codex What it means Manual Ask for approval You review permission requests. Claude asks before edits and commands; Codex already allows work inside the project and asks before crossing its access boundary. Accept edits No exact equivalent Claude allows file edits and common file commands, but asks before other commands. Codex’s Ask for approval already permits project edits and commands within its limits. Auto Approve for me Automatic checks handle routine approval decisions. Some actions still need you. In Codex, the project’s access limits stay in place. Bypass permissions Full access Removes major approval or access restrictions. These are broader than automatic review; they are not needed just to reduce routine prompts.

Planning is a separate choice. Claude’s Plan mode explores and proposes an approach without editing your source files. In Codex, ask the agent to show you a read-only setting if you want to prevent edits. Simply asking for a plan in a message does not change permissions.

For more detail, see the Claude permission guide or Codex permission guide.

Anecdotally, I think Auto in Claude or Approve for me in Codex is the right permission setting for most users. For folders and documents I don’t want the agent to have access to, I keep them in the cloud and not locally synced. I also keep them out of the cloud connections I give the agent access to.

I understand the access and approval settings for this session.

docs.title: 4. Pick a project and open its folder
docs.text:
A folder is your project’s home. Always work in a project.

My project folders are relatively coarse. I typically have one for each research project I’m working on, one for AI workflows, and one for family, home, and personal matters. You can nest sub-projects inside those folders. For example, I might keep a Family vacation folder inside Home. When I want to work on the vacation, I point the agent to that subfolder rather than the broader Home folder.

Open the top-level folder for the work you want to do. For a whole research project, that means the folder containing its writing, figures, and other subfolders. For the family vacation, it means the vacation folder. Give the agent the project’s home, rather than opening one file at a time.

You can also organize work into projects in the Claude and Codex apps and give a working session access to multiple folders. For example, one of my research assistants might have a Codex project for a research study that brings together:

  • A Dropbox folder for project management and writing.
  • A local GitHub repository folder for code.
  • A Box folder for data.

Those folders can stay where they are. Add their locally available folders to the same project or session so the agent can work across them.

ClaudeCodex

Start a local Code session and select your project folder below the message box. To add another folder during the session, use + → Add folder. You can also save a multi-folder environment for later sessions. See Claude’s folder controls for details.

Add a local project and attach its folder. Use Edit project → Add folder to attach more folders, and Make primary to choose where new chats start. Start a new chat inside that project. See Projects and chats for the current controls.

I’ve opened my project and attached its working folders.

docs.title: 5. Tell it what you need and let it ask questions
docs.text:
Explain the result you want, the decision you need to make, and your constraints. Point to the relevant files. Then have it grill you about the information it still needs. You can dictate this in whatever order it comes to you.

Not sure what type of task to start with? Here are a few ideas: plan a family vacation, organize your health and fitness, compare options for a household purchase, prepare for a meeting and draft the follow-up, catch up on a research or work project, or review your week and decide what to tackle next.

Here are two examples of how to ask. Use the one closer to your work, or substitute your own task.

A funder presentationA family trip 
I need help building a slide deck for a funder. My initial rough thoughts, figures, and earlier proposals are scattered throughout this folder. My previous correspondence with them is in Gmail. The slide deck should be about 20 slides. Read the relevant material and help me think through what the right structure and flow would be. Is there any other information you need from me, or that we need to gather? Ask me the questions that would change your recommendation. Once you’ve suggested a rough flow, you can take the first pass at building it in PowerPoint.

Help me plan a family trip. Start with the general notes in this folder about my typical budgets and what we like doing. The whole family is coming and we’re thinking about going sometime in August, but our dates are flexible. Before we start searching options, ask what else you need to know about us. Help me compare a few realistic options and decide which trade-offs matter.

For either task, the first exchange helps the agent understand the job. It should come back with questions, an approach, or an initial piece of work you can react to.

For the highest quality work, I use a council of agents to approach the job independently, then synthesize the dominant approaches. You can read more in the council guide, the second step in the starter guide.

I’ve explained a meaningful task and supplied the context it needs.

docs.title: 6. Work back and forth
docs.text:
Some people plan and execute. Other people iterate back and forth. Either way, get used to having the conversation. You supply information, answer questions, read what the agent produces, and give it another direction.

If the proposed flow for the funder deck is unclear, ask:

Walk me through the story you’re proposing for this deck. What should the funder understand by the end, and what are we asking them to support? Use our previous correspondence to explain why you chose this emphasis. What’s missing before you build the slides?

When it produces a draft, tell it what you don’t like and what you do like. Be specific about what needs to change. For the funder deck:

The opening is too abstract. Start with the problem the funder cares about and move the background later. Keep the results figure, but simplify the labels and explain the takeaway in the slide title. Use our latest email exchange to make the funding ask more concrete. Revise the PowerPoint and keep it to about 20 slides.

Open the PowerPoint itself. Look at the flow, figures, and slide layouts. Ask about anything you do not understand, and go back and forth until you have a deck you’re happy with.

I’ve given feedback, inspected the revised work and checked the important claims.

docs.title: 7. Save where you landed
docs.text:
Make the second session easy to start. Before you finish, ask:

Save the work in this project folder and write HANDOFF.md with the current status, decisions, links to the files, unresolved questions and next step. Show me where you saved it.

Open the handoff. Tomorrow, return to the same project and ask the agent to read HANDOFF.md and pick up where we left off. Correct anything that changed since you last worked on it.

The work and a useful handoff are saved in my project.

docs.title: Before you use this on real work
docs.text: Keeping files on your computer does not mean everything happens there. Content the agent reads may be sent to its provider or a connected service to do the work. Use your organization’s approved setup for restricted records. For more detail, read how the data flows.

docs.title: Are you asking multiple subagents to tackle the task?
docs.text:
I use councils and adversarial review as the default for essentially every task and every review. Instead of settling for one AI’s first answer, I want several independent attempts and a synthesis of what they found. One agent may see an approach, another a missing assumption, and another a reason to ask a different question.

The habit is simple: describe the task, let a council work on it, add your judgment, and improve the result. Use /council to develop the work, then /adversarial-review to examine the result, along with your own judgment. Additional review cycles are choices you can add as needed.

Not sure what subagents are?

When you chat with an AI in Claude Code or Codex, that’s your main agent. The separate workers it starts and manages behind the scenes are subagents. Subagents are particularly useful when you want to tackle many things in parallel. A council asks several of them to tackle the same question independently, then brings their findings together. Adversarial review asks fresh workers to examine the result independently and find consequential problems.

A skill is a saved set of instructions for your agent. The /council skill prepares the members’ assignment, coordinates their work, and arranges the synthesis. The slash helps you invoke the skill directly. You can also ask in plain language: “Use the council skill to help me with this task.” The agent can recognize the request, load the installed skill, and spin up the subagents.

A plugin bundles skills and their supporting files so you can install them together, once. There’s more on agents and skills if you want it.

docs.title: The working loop
docs.text:
We’re going to start by assuming you have only one AI subscription, and the council skill in the starter kit works by spinning up subagents with different personas to tackle the task.

Your request goes into /council, which prepares the shared brief, sends it to three independent members, and arranges a synthesis. You ask questions, give your judgment, and have the draft revised. Then /adversarial-review brings in four fresh reviewers. Use their findings to edit again, and save a handoff when you finish.

The simple council loop Your request, council, add judgment and revise, adversarial review, check and revise again if needed, then done. Before starting a new request, read HANDOFF.md. Your request /council Add judgment and revise /adversarial-review Check and revise again if needed /done Read HANDOFF.md, then start a new request See how each skill uses subagents for several independent attempts Council and adversarial review loop Your session invokes council: three separate subagents, Skeptic, Pre-mortem, and Completeness Checker, converge on a separate synthesis subagent. Your judgment and draft revision lead to adversarial-review: four fresh separate subagents, Skeptic, Pre-mortem, Completeness Checker, and Chief of Staff, converge on a fresh synthesis subagent. Your session revises and checks, then invokes done. A return arrow allows another revision cycle. Revise again, if needed /council /adversarial-review Fresh subagents Your request Skeptic Pre-mortem Completeness Checker Synthesis Your judgment Revise draft Skeptic Pre-mortem Completeness Checker Chief of Staff Synthesis Revise & check /done Your sessionSeparate subagent

Next: connect different AI models and change your default council →

docs.title: 1. Install the starter kit
docs.text:
You’ll want a council skill to follow the rest of this workflow. You can ask for a council manually each time, but it’s not practical to keep rebuilding the instructions. A repeatable skill gives the agents a consistent process to follow.

Andrej Karpathy’s LLM Council inspired my council setup. I also bring in fresh reviewers after I’ve had a chance to weigh in.

I’m not the only one doing this, and you do not have to use my skills. The advantage of mine is that the workflows and guides on this website refer to them, so the examples should be easier to follow. The tradeoff is upkeep: I get bogged down by other tasks and I might forget to update the skill bundle online. Other authors may maintain theirs more actively. Here’s a list of other council and adversarial review skills others have published.

What the starter kit adds

The starter kit is a self-contained bundle of the seven skills below and their supporting files. The other skills in my GitHub repository are separate—you can add them later if you want.

Command What it does /council Develops the work with independent members and synthesizes their findings. /adversarial-review Reviews the draft with a fresh panel and synthesizes its findings. /kit-hello, /kit-setup Checks the installation, introduces the skills, and connects other agents. Usually needed only during setup. /ask-agents Asks another connected agent for an outside opinion. /prompt Helps you prepare or improve a prompt, and carries out the task when you ask it to. /done Saves a handoff for your next session.

Codex installation: Starter Kit for Codex plugin and installation instructions Claude installation: Starter Kit for Claude plugin and installation instructions

I publish some of my other frequently used skills on GitHub, if and when you want them.

For installation (and anything else): when in doubt, just ask the AI to do it. That’s a general principle for making the most of AI. The rest of the page is here if you’re interested in what’s happening or want more detail, but ideally, we don’t actually want you to follow all the instructions. We want your AI to follow them.

Open a local Claude Code or Codex session, navigate to the project you want to work in, and ask your agent something as simple as this:

Walk me through the councils page on claudeblattman.com. I want to install the starter kit. Then explain to me what it is.

You don’t have to learn the installation procedure before you start. Ask it to install it and teach you. You may still need to click an install button, approve access, or sign in yourself.

If that didn’t work, install the starter kit manually as a plugin ClaudeCodex
  1. Open the Claude app’s Settings → Plugins. In versions with a Customize section, look for Customize → Plugins instead.
  2. Choose Add → Add Marketplace → Add from a repository. Enter https://github.com/chrisblattman/claudeblattman and select Sync.
  3. Find starter-kit, open it, and choose Install.
  4. Start a new Code session in your project folder. Type /kit-hello and select the matching skill from the suggestions. The app fills in the plugin prefix. Send it to check that the plugin responds.
  1. Open Plugins in the app’s sidebar, or Settings → Plugins in versions that put it there.
  2. Search for Starter Kit for Codex, open its details, and choose Install or the + button. If it is not listed, give the agent the GitHub repository link so it can check the repository installation route.
  3. Start a new chat in your project folder. Type /kit-hello, select the matching skill, and send it to check the installation.

If the controls in your version look different, use the current Claude installation guide or Codex plugins guide, or ask the agent to walk you through them.

Running into an excessive amount of permission requests?

The quick answer: turn on automatic permissions to reduce routine approval prompts—Auto in Claude Code or Approve for me in Codex, where available. These modes check actions automatically, though some requests may still need your approval. Ask your agent to show you the setting, then read Set permissions in Your first session for more about what it allows and how to choose your settings.

The skills and their supporting files are installed.

docs.title: 2. Meet the council
docs.text:
The starter kit’s council uses three independent subagents of the same AI, with different personas, or assigned perspectives:

Persona Its assignment Skeptic Find important claims that lack support and explain the evidence gap. Pre-mortem Imagine the plan failed. Identify the top three concrete causes and a mitigation for each. Completeness Checker Find gaps against standard practice: people who need to be involved, dependencies, inputs, and success criteria.

These are separate subagents, each considering the whole task through its assigned lens.

My own default uses one Claude agent, one Codex agent, and one Gemini agent. I find the differences between models useful. Part two explains how to connect different agents and change your default. You can start here with the AI you already use.

I understand what the three members will examine.

docs.title: 3. Give the council one real task
docs.text:
Choose something you actually need: a proposal, a decision, a draft, or an approach to a new project. Start a session in your project folder, then type or dictate in ordinary language. For example:

/council Help me develop a two-page proposal for a second pilot. We've already done a first pilot. The information is scattered through this project folder, [other locations, such as Google Docs, email threads, etc.]. I've started discussing changes for this pilot in email with [names here]. Some questions I'm thinking about are, [list them here]. I'm worried about [concerns, constraints here].

Council organizes the dictated request under the hood into a structured PROMPT.md. You do not need to dictate in a particular order or arrive with a polished prompt. What matters is giving it the information that will make the result useful:

  • The result and its audience. What should exist at the end, who will use it, and what decision or job it needs to support.
  • The material and constraints. Where to find the relevant files; the deadline, length, budget, and requirements that must hold.
  • What good looks like. How you will judge the output. “My manager can decide without asking us to reconstruct the staffing plan” is more useful than “make it excellent.”
  • Examples and corrections. Point to a good previous result and say what to borrow. If an earlier attempt missed your intent, explain what was wrong and what should be different this time.

You can leave the method open. If you do not know how to approach the task, ask the council to suggest an approach and come back with the questions that would materially change it. You supply the goal, context, and judgment; you do not have to prescribe every step.

My first prompts in a work session are typically 3 to 4 paragraphs. You shouldn't worry about concision, and in fact the more context and information you can give the council, the better

I’ve asked the council to handle the task. My dictated message includes relevant files, constraints, and desired results.

docs.title: 4. Let the council members work independently
docs.text:
The agent you are talking to sends the shared prompt and relevant files—or access to those files—to three separate subagents. Each gets the same question and evidence, plus any assigned persona. They finish their reports independently, before seeing one another’s answers. Dividing the budget, timetable, and writing among agents can be useful too, but that is a different assignment from getting independent takes on the whole proposal.

When all three reports are back, your main agent brings them together for synthesis. It gives that job to a fresh subagent. The synthesis compares the reasons and evidence, explains the disagreements, and brings forward important findings raised by only one member. It produces one report with the recommended approach, the unresolved questions, and the decisions that need your judgment. Agreement alone does not prove a claim is true.

My three subagents ran and produced a synthesis report for me.

docs.title: 5. Ask questions and give your judgment
docs.text:
Read the synthesis. Ask for elaboration or clarification on consequential or debated points. You can ask the agent to bring forward the relevant evidence and explain why the council members disagree.

Explain the disagreement about staffing. Which assumptions drive it, what evidence supports each view, and what would change the recommendation?

You do not have to accept the recommendations verbatim. Once you have dug into the points you did not understand or agree with, say what you accept, reject, or want changed. For example, if the synthesis has numbered recommendations:

I’ve read points 4, 5, and 6; they sound fine. Reject point 1: I want to test the process with our existing customers before expanding it to new ones. Apply your suggested revision in point 9, shortening the pilot to five weeks so we have a week to deal with delays. Save the current version, then revise the proposal itself using these decisions.

Your priorities and constraints help the agent revise the actual work.

I dug into the important disagreements and have given my direction.

docs.title: 6. Run adversarial review
docs.text:
Once you’ve added your judgment, provided feedback, and pushed back where needed, use /adversarial-review to examine the revised work. It starts a fresh panel to look for consequential problems. The starter kit’s default is four independent subagents of the same AI, followed by a fresh synthesis.

Reviewer What it checks in the draft Skeptic Which important claims lack support? Where is the argument relying on wishful thinking? Pre-mortem What are the top three concrete causes of failure, and what could prevent each? Completeness Checker Who needs to be involved? What dependencies, inputs, or success criteria are missing? Which vague commitments need to be made concrete? Chief of Staff What is the actual decision, what does saying yes cost, and is it reversible? Would a smaller commitment serve you better?

The first three personas overlap with /council, but they now review the draft, using fresh reviewers who did not develop it. The Chief of Staff adds a check on whether the result helps you decide and act.

/adversarial-review Review the revised pilot proposal against my original request and the decisions we made afterward. Distinguish must-fix problems from preferences.

Just like /council, each reviewer receives the full brief and the same version of the work, plus its assigned focus.

I have reviewed the findings of the four-member panel.

docs.title: 7. Apply the changes and check them
docs.text:
Review does not, in and of itself, finish the task. Once /adversarial-review has come back, I edit again using those comments and findings. Tell the agent which findings to act on, ask it to explain any it rejects, and inspect the changed files. Go back and forth with your agent as many times as you need to get a final result you’re satisfied with.

I usually find one Council round and one Adversarial Review round, plus a few back and forth final comments, sufficient. Of course, that’s not a hard rule. A major revision, unresolved disagreement, or new evidence may justify another round. Give that round a specific question to settle.

The useful fixes are applied, and I have checked the result.

docs.title: 8. Save where you landed
docs.text:
Agentic memory is getting better, but for consequential work or long working days, use /done to save a handoff in your project folder. This is particularly helpful if you are planning to pick up work in this project in a new session rather than continuing in this one.

/done asks the agent to record the current status, decisions, unresolved questions, next action, and links to the work and council reports in HANDOFF.md. It gives the next session a route back to the task brief, individual reports, and synthesis saved with the project, so it can inspect how you reached the result.

The work and handoff are saved where I can find them.

docs.title: Next steps for intermediate and advanced users
docs.text:
Start with one useful task, then build on what worked. I've put the quick, widely useful habits first. After that, give one project a home, use it for research and meetings, and work up to routines that run regularly.

The first two stages cover the homepage essentials. If those are already familiar, start with one ongoing project. Follow the order when you're unsure what to try next, and skip tasks you've already done or don't need.

This page keeps its own checkmarks in your browser, separate from the homepage.

docs.title: Stage 1 — Learn to use an agent and run the council loop
docs.text: Choose your agent. Open a project in the desktop app. Give the agent one real task, then work through a revision together. Annotate the agent's work instead of describing the changes you want. Start using councils to tackle the task and adversarially review the output. Consider using multiple AIs in your council. It’s worth the cost!

docs.title: Stage 2 — Reduce the friction between you and your agent
docs.text: Save standing instructions about how you work and what you prefer, so they carry across projects and sessions. Dictate a request you would usually type. Transcribe a meeting. Process the transcript: file it with its project and use it for follow-ups. Teach your agent to write and sound like you. Teach the agent to learn from your edits so the next draft sounds more like you.

docs.title: Stage 3 — Give your projects reference documents
docs.text: Set up a new project or clean up an existing one so its files and decisions have one home. Write the project description or research design to use when you write proposals and reports. Build a project dashboard for current tasks, responsibilities, and decisions that need attention. Learn the pre- and post-meeting workflow. Refresh the dashboard after meetings, and update the project description when the plan changes. If scattered files are getting in your way, try a one-time cleanup of your cloud storage.

docs.title: Stage 4 — Research and analysis
docs.text: Research a real question with a research council or Deep Research, then put the findings to work.

docs.title: Stage 5 — Build your daily email routine
docs.text: Clean up your email backlog and set labels and filtering rules. Try inbox triage to sort the mail your Gmail filters haven't handled. Run a check-in to work through the messages, replies, and decisions that need you. Create your own email digest for a group of messages you'd rather read a summary of, such as school emails.

docs.title: Stage 6 — Improve your setup and save what works
docs.text:
Connect an app so your agent can do more for you. Read about outside skills I've installed that help with daily work, including Recall for finding past conversations.

Set rules and guidelines for the work you do regularly. Once a task works well and you keep repeating it, turn it into a skill. Fix or update a skill when it stops working well or your needs change. Review your skills periodically to decide what to fix, combine, or retire as agent models change. Scout and curate new AI tips to add to your workflow.

docs.title: Try agents in your personal life
docs.text: Build a personal shopper to help with a purchase you're considering. Plan a vacation. Prepare for tax season. The guide includes background on academic taxes. Get help with health and fitness.

docs.title: Use agents to help you prepare your taxes
docs.text:
Claude Blattman — not quite a CPA.

Refresh coming February 2027.

In a former life — for about six to twelve months during and after college — I was an auditor and then a tax accountant. I was not particularly good at it, and I hated every minute. But I learned enough to be dangerous: enough to do my own taxes, and enough, I think, to teach Claude Code how to take the painful pieces away.

This year I decided to use Claude Code for as much of my tax preparation as I could. I used it to assemble my charitable contributions from a sprawling Google Sheet, compile my itemized deductions from scattered receipts across email and credit card statements, and build a Schedule C for my consulting income. Some of it was still manual. I had to eyeball credit card statements to flag which charges were medical and which were childcare. But Claude Code is surprisingly good at the grunt work: sorting transactions, filtering by category, downloading and parsing CSV exports, and assembling it all into spreadsheets ready for tax software.

It also helped me think through some tax planning decisions — weighing different filing software, running a rough cost-benefit on whether hiring an accountant was worth it given how I value my time. What I did in about three hours, I would have had to pay an accountant $1,000 for.

The case study below uses fictional profiles to walk through the skills I built. AI tools in this space are moving fast — expect updated approaches next year.

This is not tax advice

Everything on these pages is educational content about AI workflow design. All dollar amounts are fictional. All examples use fictional personas. Nothing here constitutes tax, legal, or financial advice. Consult a qualified professional for your specific situation.

Don't want to read all this?

Two shortcuts:

  1. Install /tax-guide (below) and let it ask you 8 questions — it'll tell you exactly which parts apply to your situation.
  2. Point Claude Code at this page. Paste the URL https://claudeblattman.com/tax-workflow/ into a Claude Code session and ask it to walk you through the workflow based on your tax situation. It can read the site, summarize the relevant parts, and help you decide what to do.

docs.title: Start Here
docs.text: Install /tax-guide and answer 8 questions. You'll get a personalized plan: what documents to collect, whether to self-file or hire a professional, and which parts of this case study apply to you.

docs.title: Install /tax-guide
docs.text:
Install the tax-guide skill in its own Claude Code skill folder:

mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills/tax-guide
curl -fL -o ~/.claude/skills/tax-guide/SKILL.md \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chrisblattman/claudeblattman/main/skills/tax-guide/SKILL.md

Open a fresh session and type /tax-guide to start. If you already have an older tax-guide.md command, preserve your customizations and move that copy outside the active commands folder before using the replacement.

Sample output — W-2 + side consulting profile

1. RECOMMENDATION

This is manageable with tax software, but the Schedule C
requires careful expense categorization. The three-year
review step is especially important for your situation.

2. YOUR DOCUMENT CHECKLIST

3. SUGGESTED WORKFLOW

Or browse the case study directly

docs.title: Is This for You?
docs.text:
This case study is useful if any of these apply:

  • You file your own taxes (or want to understand what your preparer does)
  • You have a complicated return — consulting income, multiple 1099s, itemized deductions, investment accounts
  • You want to learn how to build Claude Code skills for document-heavy workflows
  • You're curious about where AI actually helps with sensitive personal tasks — and where it fails

You do not need to:

  • Use Claude Code for your own taxes (many shouldn't — see When to Get Help)
  • Know anything about tax law
  • Have any prior Claude Code experience (though the Build Your Own section assumes familiarity with skills)

docs.title: The Three-Sentence Version
docs.text: I built two Claude Code skills: one that searches Gmail for tax documents, downloads attachments, extracts key figures, and tracks what's still missing; and another that compiles deductions from multiple sources into spreadsheets ready for data entry. A third-year review skill compares the current return against two prior years to catch anomalies. The skills saved real time — but the biggest value was catching errors I would have missed, and the biggest lesson was learning exactly where AI needs a human checking every output.

docs.title: How to Read This
docs.text:
Fastest path: Run /tax-guide (install above) — it will tell you exactly which pages to read.

If you just want the story: Read the Workflow Overview and What AI Got Wrong. Skip the technical sections.

If you want to build something similar: Start with Privacy & Setup, then read the case study pages in order, then move to Build Your Own.

If you're an academic wondering about your own taxes: Start with Academic Tax Basics and When to Get Help.

docs.title: Privacy, Data, and Setup Decisions
docs.text:
Before using AI for anything involving tax documents, you need to make deliberate choices about what data touches which systems. This page walks through the decisions and their trade-offs.

This is not tax advice

Educational content about AI workflow design. Not tax, legal, or financial advice.

docs.title: The Core Question
docs.text: Tax preparation involves some of the most sensitive personal data you have: Social Security numbers, bank account numbers, income figures, employer details, medical information. The first decision is what you're comfortable sending through an AI system — and what stays local.

docs.title: How Data Flows in This Workflow
docs.text:
graph LR
    A[Gmail] -->|MCP reads email metadata<br>& attachment content| B[Claude Code<br>on your machine]
    C[Google Sheets] -->|MCP reads<br>spreadsheet data| B
    D[Local files<br>PDFs, CSVs] -->|Read tool| B
    B -->|Writes files| E[Local filesystem<br>your tax folder]
    B -->|API calls with<br>conversation context| F[Anthropic API]

    style F fill:#ff6b6b,color:#fff
    style E fill:#51cf66,color:#fff
    style B fill:#339af0,color:#fff

What stays local: Downloaded PDFs, generated spreadsheets, and your tax folder never leave your machine. Claude Code reads and writes them through local filesystem tools.

What goes to Anthropic's API: The conversation context — which includes any text Claude reads from your documents. When Claude reads a W-2 PDF and extracts wage figures, those figures are sent to the API as part of the conversation. Anthropic's data policy states that API inputs are not used for model training, but you should read the current policy yourself.

What goes through Google's API: Gmail MCP searches and reads emails through Google's API. Google Sheets MCP reads spreadsheet data. These follow Google's existing data handling for your account.

docs.title: Decisions to Make Before You Start
Decision 1: What data will you allow in the AI conversation?
docs.text:
Data Type Risk Level Recommendation Document types (W-2, 1099, etc.) Low Allow — needed for the workflow Dollar amounts from tax forms Medium Allow if comfortable — needed for compilation and review Employer names, payer names Medium Allow — needed for document matching Social Security numbers High Exclude — never needed for this workflow Bank account / routing numbers High Exclude — never needed for this workflow Medical provider details Medium-High Consider — needed only for medical expense compilation

The skills described in this case study are designed to never need SSNs or bank account numbers. You can add explicit instructions to your CLAUDE.md:

## Tax Document Rules
- NEVER extract, display, or store Social Security numbers
- NEVER extract, display, or store bank account or routing numbers
- If you encounter these in a document, skip past them

PDF extraction transmits sensitive data to the API

CLAUDE.md rules prevent Claude from displaying sensitive values, but they do not prevent transmission. When Claude reads a W-2 or 1099 PDF, the entire text content — including SSNs, EINs, bank account numbers, and other identifiers — is sent to Anthropic's API as part of the conversation context. To mitigate this:

  • Redact SSNs and account numbers from PDFs before giving them to Claude (use your PDF editor's redaction tool, or black out and re-save)
  • Or enter figures manually instead of using PDF extraction for documents that contain SSNs (W-2s, 1099s, 1098s)
  • Verify Anthropic's current data retention policy at anthropic.com/policies before proceeding

docs.title: Decision 2: Will you use Gmail MCP for document collection?
docs.text:
With Gmail MCP: Claude searches your email, finds tax documents, downloads attachments, and tracks what's missing. This is the core of the /tax-collect skill.

Gmail MCP grants access to your entire inbox

Gmail MCP does not scope to tax-related emails only. Once configured, Claude Code can search and read any email in your account — salary negotiations, medical correspondence, legal matters, and everything else. Consider what's in your inbox before enabling it. If this is a concern, you can create a dedicated Gmail label for tax documents and manually move emails there, then limit your skill's search to that label.

Without Gmail MCP: You download documents manually and place them in your tax folder. Claude can still compile, categorize, and review them — you just skip the automated collection step.

The Gmail MCP advantage is significant for people with scattered documents across dozens of emails. If your documents arrive in 3-4 emails, manual download is fine.

docs.title: Decision 3: Local processing vs. cloud processing
docs.text:
Everything in this workflow runs through Claude Code on your local machine talking to Anthropic's API. There is no separate cloud service, no third-party tax platform, and no data stored beyond the API conversation window.

After each session ends, Anthropic may retain API inputs for up to 30 days for safety monitoring per their current data retention policy — verify the latest terms at anthropic.com/policies before proceeding. Your local files persist.

docs.title: Setting Up Secure Document Access
docs.text: Claude Code can read any file on your local filesystem. That's powerful during tax season — and a reason to be deliberate about what's on your filesystem the rest of the year.

docs.title: The pattern: temporary access, permanent separation
docs.text:
Phase 1 — Before tax season: Keep tax documents in a location Claude Code cannot reach. This could be:

  • A cloud service that isn't synced locally (e.g., an unsynced Dropbox folder, a Box folder, iCloud Drive with selective sync disabled for that folder)
  • An encrypted disk image you only mount when needed
  • A USB drive

Your sensitive financial documents should not sit in a locally-synced folder year-round. Claude Code can access anything on your local filesystem — including cloud folders that sync automatically.

Phase 2 — During tax season: Create a dedicated working folder and bring in only the documents you need:

# Create a tax working folder
mkdir -p ~/tax-prep-2025/documents
mkdir -p ~/tax-prep-2025/output

# Copy documents from your secure location
cp "/path/to/secure-storage/W2-2025.pdf" ~/tax-prep-2025/documents/
cp "/path/to/secure-storage/1099-NEC-*.pdf" ~/tax-prep-2025/documents/

Point your tax skills at this folder. All downloads, extractions, and generated spreadsheets go here.

Phase 3 — After filing: Remove the working folder and its contents:

# Archive final output to your secure location
cp ~/tax-prep-2025/output/*.xlsx "/path/to/secure-storage/2025-filed/"

# Delete the working folder
rm -rf ~/tax-prep-2025

# Start a fresh Claude Code session (old session context
# included your tax data)

docs.title: If you use Gmail MCP for document collection
docs.text:
Gmail MCP gives Claude Code access to your entire inbox — not just tax emails. Two options if you'd rather limit exposure:

  • Enable Gmail MCP only during tax season. Add the configuration to ~/.claude.json when you're ready to collect documents, remove it when you're done. You don't need every integration running year-round.
  • Use a label-based approach. Manually move tax emails to a dedicated Gmail label, then instruct the skill to search only that label.

docs.title: What to keep out of the working folder entirely
docs.text:
Some documents should never enter Claude's reach:

  • Prior year tax returns (contain SSNs, full financial picture) — enter comparison figures manually
  • Bank statements (account numbers, transaction history beyond what's needed)
  • Estate or trust documents (beneficiary SSNs, asset details)

If a skill needs a figure from one of these, open the document yourself and type the number in. The 30 seconds of manual entry is worth the privacy gain.

docs.title: Pre-Flight Privacy Checklist
docs.text:
Run through this before your first tax session:

  • [ ] Read Anthropic's current data policy — confirm API inputs are not used for training
  • [ ] Add SSN/bank exclusion rules to your CLAUDE.md (see above)
  • [ ] Decide on Gmail MCP — will you use automated email search, or download documents manually?
  • [ ] Create a dedicated tax working folder — a local folder (e.g., ~/tax-prep-2025/) that you'll delete after filing. See Setting Up Secure Document Access above.
  • [ ] Verify your tax documents aren't in a synced folder — if they're in Dropbox, iCloud, or Google Drive, are those folders synced locally? If so, Claude Code can already read them.
  • [ ] Review who has access to your machine — anyone who can open Claude Code can access your conversation history
  • [ ] Plan your cleanup — after filing, delete the working folder, archive output to your secure location, and start a fresh Claude Code session

docs.title: Post-Season Cleanup Checklist
docs.text:
After you've filed your return:

  • [ ] Archive final output — copy generated spreadsheets and summaries to your secure storage location
  • [ ] Delete the working folder — rm -rf ~/tax-prep-2025 (or wherever you created it)
  • [ ] Disable Gmail MCP if you enabled it only for tax season — remove or comment out the entry in ~/.claude.json
  • [ ] Start a fresh session — your tax data was in the conversation context. Starting fresh ensures it's not carried into unrelated work.
  • [ ] Verify no stray copies — check your Downloads folder, Desktop, and any cloud sync folders for documents you may have opened outside the working directory

docs.title: What This Workflow Does NOT Do
docs.text:
• Does not file your taxes. It organizes documents and compiles data. You enter figures into tax software yourself.
  • Does not connect to the IRS, tax software, or financial institutions. All data comes from your email and local files.
  • Does not store tax data persistently. Each Claude Code session starts fresh. Your local files are the only persistent record.
  • Does not make tax decisions. It presents data for your review. Classification of deductions, income categorization, and filing decisions are yours.

docs.title: Tool Requirements
docs.text:
To replicate the full workflow described in this case study, you need:

Tool Required for Setup guide Claude Code Everything Install the desktop app Gmail MCP Document collection from email MCP Setup Google Sheets MCP Charitable contribution export MCP Setup openpyxl (Python) Generating formatted spreadsheets pip3 install openpyxl

Minimum viable setup: Claude Code + local files only. You can still use the compilation and review patterns without any MCP integrations — just download documents manually.

Next: The Workflow Overview — how the full pipeline works, and meet the fictional personas.

docs.title: Architecture Patterns for Your Own Workflows
docs.text:
The tax workflow uses patterns that apply to any document-heavy, multi-source, verification-critical task. This page extracts those patterns so you can build your own version — for taxes, expense reporting, grant management, or anything else that involves collecting scattered documents and turning them into organized, verified output.

This is not tax advice

Educational content about AI workflow design.

docs.title: Pattern 1: The Collection-Compilation-Review Pipeline
docs.text:
Every document workflow follows the same three-stage pipeline:

graph LR
    A["Collect<br>(find & gather)"] --> B["Compile<br>(organize & structure)"]
    B --> C["Review<br>(compare & verify)"]
    C -->|errors found| B
    C -->|gaps found| A

    style A fill:#339af0,color:#fff
    style B fill:#339af0,color:#fff
    style C fill:#339af0,color:#fff

Each stage is a separate skill. This is deliberate — you want to run collection multiple times as documents arrive, compilation once when everything is gathered, and review as a final check. Bundling them into one skill would force you to re-collect every time you want to re-compile.

Feedback loops are built in. Review can send you back to compilation (fix an error) or collection (find a missing document). These loops are how the workflow self-corrects.

docs.title: Skeleton
docs.text:
# /my-collect

Search [data source] for [document types].
For each found:
  1. Present metadata for user approval
  2. Download/save with consistent naming
  3. Extract key fields
  4. User verifies extracted data
  5. Update tracking checklist

Show completeness dashboard.
Compare against prior period to catch gaps.

# /my-compile [sub-command]

Read collected documents.
For each compilation target:
  1. Pull data from relevant sources
  2. Apply categorization (automated or guided)
  3. Generate formatted output
  4. Show summary for verification
  5. Map output to downstream entry points

# /my-review

Read current output + N prior-period outputs.
Extract key metrics.
Display side-by-side comparison.
Flag: >X% change, sign reversals, missing items.
Generate action items for investigation.

docs.title: Pattern 2: The Tracking Checklist
docs.text: A living document that records what's been collected, what's missing, and what requires manual action.

docs.title: Design Principles
docs.text:
1. Machine-readable format. Use consistent markers (✅, ⏳, 🌐) that the skill can parse programmatically.
  2. Single source of truth. One file tracks everything. Don't split across multiple files.
  3. Append-only updates. The skill adds checkmarks and notes but never removes entries. Deletion requires human action.
  4. Portal fallback section. For items that can't be automated, include URLs and instructions.

docs.title: Template
docs.text:
# Document Checklist — [Period]

## Collected
- [x] Document Type - Source — [extracted key figure]
- [x] Document Type - Source — [extracted key figure]

## Outstanding
- [ ] Document Type - Source — Expected by [date]
- [ ] Document Type - Source — Expected by [date]

## Manual Downloads Required
- [ ] Portal Name: Document Type
  → URL: [direct link to document page]
  → Credentials: [where to find login]

## Notes
- [Date]: [observation about a document or process]

docs.title: Pattern 3: The Guided Interview
docs.text: For data that requires human judgment to categorize, use a structured interview instead of automated classification.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text: Situation Use automated classification Use guided interview Clear categories, unambiguous data ✅ — Ambiguous categories, context-dependent — ✅ High-stakes decisions (tax, legal, medical) — ✅ High volume, low stakes ✅ — Mixed: some clear, some ambiguous Automated with "uncertain" bucket + human review —

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
──────────────────────────────────────
CATEGORY [N] — [DESCRIPTION]
──────────────────────────────────────
Prior period: [reference amount]
Prompts: [questions to help user recall items]

Enter items for this category.
Format: [description], [amount], [optional fields]
Type "done" when finished.
Type "skip" if nothing in this category.
Type "same" to copy prior period (you'll review them).

>

Key elements:

  • Prior period reference provides context and catches omissions (if you had $5K last year and $0 this year, that's worth investigating)
  • Prompts are domain-specific questions that jog memory ("Which conferences did you attend?" rather than "Enter travel expenses")
  • "Same" option for stable categories that rarely change between periods
  • Format specification ensures consistent parsing

docs.title: Pattern 4: The Threshold Gate
docs.text:
Before doing expensive work, check whether the result will matter.

graph TD
    A[Calculate threshold<br>from available data] --> B[Ask for rough estimate]
    B --> C{Estimate significantly<br>exceeds threshold?}
    C -->|Yes| D[Proceed with full work]
    C -->|No| E[Report: not worth pursuing<br>Time saved: ~X hours]
    C -->|Close| F[Warn and let user decide]

    style C fill:#ff922b,color:#fff

Where this applies:

  • Medical expense deduction (7.5% AGI threshold)
  • Itemized vs. standard deduction comparison
  • Any optional section where the setup cost may exceed the benefit
  • Data processing tasks with known minimum-value thresholds

Implementation tip: Always include a margin above the threshold. Estimates are rough. If the threshold is $10,000 and the estimate is $10,500, the full calculation might come in under $10,000 — wasting the user's time.

docs.title: Pattern 5: The Three-Tier Classification
docs.text:
For automated categorization of mixed-quality data (like credit card transactions), use three tiers instead of two:

Tier Rule Action Auto-qualify Strong keyword match against known-good patterns Include without human review Auto-exclude Strong keyword match against known-bad patterns Exclude without human review Uncertain No strong match, or conflicting signals Present for human review

Why three tiers beat two: A two-tier system (qualify/exclude) forces every item into a category, which maximizes false positives and false negatives. The third tier captures the genuinely ambiguous cases and sends them to a human, reducing error rates significantly.

Tuning over time: Each year (or period), review the items that ended up in "uncertain" and add their patterns to the auto-qualify or auto-exclude lists. The uncertain bucket should shrink over time.

docs.title: Pattern 6: The Historical Comparison
docs.text: Compare current output against N prior periods to catch anomalies that are invisible in a single-period view.

docs.title: Anomaly Detection Rules
docs.text: Rule What it catches Threshold Percentage change Gradual drift or sudden jumps >15% year-over-year Sign reversal Profit → loss or vice versa Any sign change Missing items Sources present last period but not this one Any absence New items Sources present this period but not last Flag for attention Ratio changes Proportions between categories shifting >5 percentage points

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
For each metric in [defined list]:
  1. Extract value from current period
  2. Extract value from N prior periods
  3. Calculate year-over-year change
  4. Apply anomaly rules
  5. Flag any triggers

Display: side-by-side table with change column
Group flags by severity:
  !! = investigate before proceeding
  !  = note and verify
  (blank) = normal variation

docs.title: Pattern 7: The Entry Guide
docs.text: Map compiled data to downstream input fields. This bridges the gap between "organized data" and "data entry."

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
The most error-prone step in any compilation workflow is not the compilation itself — it's the manual entry of compiled data into a downstream system. Misreading a spreadsheet cell, entering a value in the wrong field, or transposing digits.

The entry guide reduces this risk by listing each value alongside the exact field where it belongs.

docs.title: Template
docs.text:
ENTRY GUIDE — [System Name]
──────────────────────────────────────

Navigation                        Value
──────────────────────────        ──────────
[Section] > [Sub-section]
  [Field name]                    $XX,XXX
  [Field name]                    $X,XXX
  [Field name]                    $XXX

[Section] > [Sub-section]
  [Field name]                    $XX,XXX

docs.title: Putting It Together
docs.text:
Here's how these patterns combine for a non-tax example — expense reporting:

/expense-collect
├── Search email for receipts (Pattern 1: Collection)
├── Track against expense policy categories (Pattern 2: Checklist)
├── Classify vendor types (Pattern 5: Three-tier)
└── Compare against prior months (Pattern 6: Historical)

/expense-compile
├── Categorize by project and expense type (Pattern 3: Guided interview)
├── Check against per-diem limits (Pattern 4: Threshold gate)
├── Generate formatted report (Pattern 1: Compilation)
└── Map to expense system fields (Pattern 7: Entry guide)

/expense-review
├── Compare against budget forecast (Pattern 6: Historical)
└── Flag unusual patterns (Pattern 6: Anomaly detection)

To build your own: Start with Pattern 1 (the pipeline structure), add Pattern 2 (tracking), then layer in whichever other patterns your domain requires.

docs.title: Pattern 8: The Validation Stack
docs.text:
AI tools are most dangerous when they're confidently wrong. Reliable workflows use multiple validation layers, each catching a different class of error:

Extraction transmits document contents to the API

Every file Claude reads — PDFs, CSVs, spreadsheet exports — is sent to Anthropic's API as conversation context. Redact sensitive identifiers (SSNs, EINs, account numbers) before processing. See Privacy & Setup.

Layer Principle Key technique Source verification Every extracted value verified against its original Display extracted data with source reference; flag low-confidence extractions from scanned documents Internal consistency Numbers should add up Cross-reference totals (sum of parts = whole); check type and magnitude Historical comparison Current period broadly consistent with prior periods Year-over-year flagging (>15% change, sign reversals, missing items); payer reconciliation Human review Contextual errors require real-world knowledge Mandatory blocking gates before final output; anomaly narratives with investigation guidance

No single layer is sufficient. Source verification catches extraction errors but not categorization errors. Historical comparison catches anomalies but not consistent mistakes. Human review catches everything in theory but misses things in practice because humans skim. The layers reinforce each other.

docs.title: Minimum viable validation
docs.text:
For any skill that extracts or compiles data, add at minimum:

  1. Display extracted values with source references (Layer 1)
  2. Sum-check any computed totals (Layer 2)
  3. Block before final output with human approval (Layer 4)

For high-stakes workflows, add historical comparison (Layer 3), confidence scoring, and anomaly narratives with investigation guidance. See What AI Got Wrong for how these layers work in practice.

Design for distrust. PDF extraction fails silently — it returns plausible wrong numbers. Categorization errors look reasonable. Missing data produces results that look complete. Every output should earn confidence through verification, not receive it by default.

docs.title: Starter Templates
docs.text:
Downloadable skill skeletons and templates you can adapt for your own document-collection and compilation workflows. These are generic — they use the architecture patterns from the tax workflow but are not tax-specific.

How to use these

Copy the template that matches your use case. Replace the bracketed fields with your domain-specific content. Save as a .md file in ~/.claude/commands/. See the skills on GitHub for installation details.

docs.title: Template 1: Document Collector
docs.text:
A skill that searches email for documents, downloads them, and tracks completeness. Adapted from the tax collection skill but generalized for any document type.

Full template — click to expand 
# /[domain]-collect — [Domain] Document Collection

*v1.0 — [date] — Initial version*

Search Gmail for [document type] documents. Download, rename,
extract key data, and track completeness.

## Arguments

- `period:[value]` — Collection period (default: [sensible default])
- `scan-only` — Preview findings without downloading

## Prerequisites

- Gmail MCP connected
- Document folder exists at `[path]/[period]/`
- Tracking checklist exists at `[path]/[period]/CHECKLIST.md`

## Instructions

### Step 1: Load Configuration

1. Parse arguments. Set `DOC_DIR` = `[path]/[period]/`
2. Read `DOC_DIR/CHECKLIST.md`
3. Display current status dashboard

### Step 2: Search Gmail

Run these searches in parallel:

#### 2a: Broad keyword search
```
"[keyword1] OR [keyword2] OR [keyword3]" after:[start] before:[end]
```

#### 2b: Known sender search
For each sender in [known sender list]:
```
from:[sender] after:[start]
```

#### 2c: Catch-all search
```
"[broader terms]" after:[start] before:[end]
```

### Step 3: Present Findings

For each email with a potential document:
```
──────────────────────────────────────
Document [N] of [Total]
──────────────────────────────────────
From: [sender]
Subject: [subject]
Date: [date]
Attachment: [filename] or "No attachment"

Document type: [classification]
Already collected? [Yes/No]

[D] Download  [S] Skip  [Q] Quit
──────────────────────────────────────
```

### Step 4: Download and Process

For each approved download:
1. Download attachment via Gmail MCP
2. Rename to consistent format: `[Type] - [Source].[ext]`
3. Extract key fields: [list fields relevant to your domain]
4. Display extracted data for user verification
5. Update CHECKLIST.md

### Step 5: Summary Dashboard

```
This session: Downloaded [N], Skipped [M]
Total collected: [X] of [Y]
Still missing: [list]
```

### Step 6: Gap Analysis

Compare current collection against prior period.
Flag any sources present last period but missing now.

## Error Handling

- Gmail MCP unavailable: Exit with message
- Download fails: Offer skip or retry
- Document unreadable: Flag for manual review

docs.title: Template 2: Compilation Skill with Guided Interview
docs.text:
A skill that compiles data from multiple sources through a structured interview. Adapted from the Schedule C compilation pattern.

Full template — click to expand 
# /[domain]-compile — [Domain] Data Compilation

*v1.0 — [date] — Initial version*

Compile [output type] from collected documents and user input
through a guided interview.

## Arguments

## Sub-commands

| Sub-command | What it does | Data source |

## Instructions

### Setup

1. Parse sub-command and period argument
2. Set `DOC_DIR` = `[path]/[period]/`
3. Verify documents exist

### Sub-command: [cmd1]

#### Step 1: Pull Data from Collected Documents

Read [document type] and extract [fields].
Display for verification:
```
[CATEGORY] (from collected documents):
  [Source 1]: [value]
  [Source 2]: [value]
  TOTAL: [sum]

Verify correct? [Y/edit/n]
```

#### Step 2: Reference Prior Period

Display prior period's [output type] for context.

#### Step 3: Guided Interview

Walk through each [category type]:

Enter items. Type "done" when finished.

## Error Handling

docs.title: Template 3: Multi-Period Review
docs.text:
A skill that compares the current period's output against prior periods to catch anomalies.

Full template — click to expand 
# /[domain]-review — [Domain] Period Comparison

*v1.0 — [date] — Initial version*

Compare current period against [N] prior periods.
Flag anomalies and generate action items.

## Arguments

- `periods:[N]` — Number of prior periods to compare (default: 2)

## Instructions

### Step 1: Locate Period Files

Search for output files in:
```
[path]/[current]/  → [filename or "not found"]
[path]/[prior-1]/  → [filename or "not found"]
[path]/[prior-2]/  → [filename or "not found"]
```

### Step 2: Extract Key Metrics

Read all period files in parallel. Extract:

| Metric | [P-2] | [P-1] | [Current] |
|--------|-------|-------|-----------|
| [Metric 1] | | | |
| [Metric 2] | | | |
| [Metric 3] | | | |

### Step 3: Anomaly Detection

For each metric, flag:
- Change > [threshold]%
- Sign reversal
- Missing in current but present in prior
- New in current but absent from prior

Display with severity:
```
!! [Metric]: [value change] — [investigation guidance]
!  [Metric]: [value change] — [note]
```

### Step 4: Action Items

Based on flags, generate:
- Items to verify before finalizing
- Items to investigate (may indicate errors)
- Items to note (expected changes)

docs.title: Compilation, Categorization, and Multi-Year Review
docs.text:
This page covers the second skill — how collected documents become organized spreadsheets ready for tax software entry. The underlying pattern is "multi-source compilation with validation": gathering data from different formats and sources, structuring it consistently, and then cross-checking the result against historical data.

This is not tax advice

Educational content about AI workflow design. All examples use fictional personas with fictional amounts.

Each sub-command is independent. You can run schedule-c without running charitable. You can run review before or after compilation. The outputs are standalone spreadsheets that reference each other but don't depend on each other.

docs.title: Schedule C: The Guided Interview Pattern
docs.text:
The Schedule C compilation is deliberately not automated. It's a structured interview where the skill asks questions and you provide answers.

Why not automate it? Because expense categorization requires judgment that AI can't reliably make:

  • Is this trip for consulting or reimbursed by your employer?
  • Is this software for your consulting business or your day job?
  • Is this a professional development purchase (deductible) or personal interest (not deductible)?

The skill provides structure: it walks through each IRS expense category, shows what you claimed last year for context, prompts with relevant questions, and handles the arithmetic (including foreign currency conversion). You provide the knowledge.

docs.title: The Interview Flow
docs.text:
Step 1: Pull 1099 income from collected documents
   └── Display gross receipts for verification

Step 2: Show prior year reference
   └── Display last year's Schedule C categories and totals

Step 3: Walk through each expense category
   ├── Line 11: Contract labor
   ├── Line 22: Supplies
   ├── Line 24a: Travel (special handling)
   ├── Line 24b: Meals (50% deductible)
   ├── Line 27a: Software & fees
   ├── Line 27b: Books
