  • Complex MCP/API setup for services with low file counts — if a service has <50 files, screenshots are faster than configuring an integration

docs.title: Tools Used
docs.text: Tool What It Did Claude Code filesystem access Local disk scanning, reading reports, editing config files Shell commands (du, df, ps, pkill) Disk usage analysis, process management Dropbox API (via Python SDK) Cloud storage inventory — 630K files enumerated Google Workspace MCP Drive file listing, trash operations, Sheets creation, Gmail osascript Apple Reminders creation, Notes search Web search Researching app behavior, integration options Screenshot reading Cataloging Box folders without API access

docs.title: Reproducible Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Create a working directory for the project
  • [ ] Run local disk audit (no setup needed)
  • [ ] Act on quick wins: delete caches, old downloads, hidden app bloat
  • [ ] Set up cloud API access (Dropbox token, Google MCP, etc.)
  • [ ] Run cloud storage inventory
  • [ ] Optimize selective sync based on active-vs-archive data
  • [ ] Inventory and clean Google Drive (or equivalent)
  • [ ] Catalog remaining cloud services (screenshots if no API)
  • [ ] Cross-reference for duplicates across services
  • [ ] Create master inventory file for AI awareness
  • [ ] Update system instructions with file location map
  • [ ] Create project index files for top active projects
  • [ ] Write cleanup instructions for other machines (if applicable)
  • [ ] Investigate integration options for remaining services

Guide created: February 12, 2026 Based on file management sessions using Claude Code (Opus 4.6)

docs.title: Coding rules
docs.text:

This page will cover standing instructions for when an agent writes code: which language and packages to use, what the agent may run on its own, and how results get checked before you rely on them. For now, the general guide to rules and guidelines applies. The AI resources for economists include coding tools from other researchers.

docs.title: Are you using 2–4 different AI models?
docs.text:
My default council is more than one AI. I ask different models to work on the same task, rather than assigning different personas to the same AI as on the first page. I find that they make different suggestions from one another.

At the time of writing (October 2026), my top choices are Claude, Codex by OpenAI (ChatGPT), and Antigravity by Google (Gemini). I use all three. I do most of my own work in Codex at the moment, for reasons I explain on the setup page. Start by getting an inexpensive, lower-tier subscription to a second AI for your high-value tasks. Try it for a month, then decide whether it’s worth purchasing a higher-tier subscription to use for all your tasks, or even subscribing to a third. I also have an inexpensive Grok subscription for specific questions every so often.

docs.title: Why would I spend money on this?
docs.text:
Think about the most important thing you have to do this month. How much would you be willing to pay for it to be done 20% better or 30% faster (or both!)?

The value of an hour of time and the value of a task will be different for everyone, but my suspicion is that it’s likely more than $23. It may well be worth more than $100 or even $200. Now think about all the other important tasks you could use it for over the course of the month.

I tend to think about this in terms of the cost of a research assistant: how much more they can accomplish in a day, or which tasks I can accomplish without their help. You can think about it in terms of your own hourly wage, or even how many coffees you buy in a month.

docs.title: What is each model good at?
docs.text:
Claude and Codex: Both are good generalists. I give them much the same jobs and often get similar answers. Codex seems a little better at web searches. I also get a lot of use out of ChatGPT's Deep Research, so I have another reason to keep that subscription.

Gemini: This is the one I keep in the council because it often comes back with something different. Claude and Codex can leave the same gaps. Gemini helps me see what they might have missed.

Grok: I pay for a small subscription mostly for searching X/Twitter. It is the best tool I've found for that, and a lot of the new AI tools and ways of using them turn up there first. I send it narrow questions about connecting tools or improving how I use them. I don't usually give it a whole project or a seat on the council.

Continue with the next-steps checklist →

docs.title: 1. Download the apps
docs.text:
Our general advice is to always ask your AI to do this for you. In this case, your AI might be able to help you download the apps using its in-app browser tools.

That said, this is one part of AI setup that I think may be easier to do manually. Download the second app you want to try, choose the version for your computer, and sign in:

  • Download Claude.
  • Download ChatGPT, which includes Codex.
  • Download Google Antigravity, which I use to work with Gemini.

I’ve installed and signed in to the apps I want to use.

docs.title: 2. Connect another model
docs.text:
Once again, ask your AI to do this for you. Keep working in the app you prefer. Your main agent will call the other agents and bring their answers back into your conversation.

Open a session in the project folder you used on the first page. If you have not installed the starter kit, do that first. Then ask something as simple as:

I want to connect the other AI apps to this app. I think there are instructions on claudeblattman.com. Walk me through it.

Or tell it exactly what you want to connect:

I want to connect [app 2] and [app 3] to [main app you are currently in]. I want you to be able to call agents and subagents from those apps, collect the information, and bring it back to this app.
If you need the steps, connect the agents with /kit-setup ClaudeCodex
  1. Start a Code session in your project folder.
  2. Type /kit-setup, select the matching skill from the suggestions, and send it.
  3. Choose which agents you want to connect when asked. The kit checks which other AI agents are available and walks you through the connections, including any installation or sign-in steps.
  4. Wait for confirmation that the connection works before moving on.
  1. Start a local chat in your project folder.
  2. Type /kit-setup, select the matching skill from the suggestions, and send it.
  3. Choose which agents you want to connect when asked. The kit checks which other AI agents are available and walks you through the connections, including any installation or sign-in steps.
  4. Wait for confirmation that the connection works before moving on.

I am cross-agent connected!

docs.title: 3. Ask a quick question with /ask-agents
docs.text:
I use /ask-agents for a quick, specific request or question: check an assumption, explain a disagreement, or give an outside opinion on one part of a draft. I still use /council to tackle entire tasks.

Try an outside opinion on the pilot proposal from the first page. Ask the other AI you connected. For example, if that is Claude:

/ask-agents Ask Claude to read the second-pilot proposal and the concerns and constraints in my original request. What is the most important question my manager should ask before approving it? Explain why it matters and point to the relevant part of the proposal. Tell me which model answered and whether it could read the proposal itself.

Replace “Claude” with the agent you connected. Use the sample proposal or another document suitable for sending to that service. The starter kit’s outside-agent helpers are not for confidential or sensitive records.

Read the response. Does it reveal a problem you missed? If it does, ask your main agent to investigate and revise the proposal. If you disagree, explain why and ask it to examine the objection. For example:

Check that concern against the staffing notes. If it holds up, revise the proposal and show me what changed. If it does not, explain what the reviewer missed.

If the connection is not working, you can still do this manually: ask your main agent to prepare a self-contained brief, including the file paths for relevant material. Paste the brief into the other app with access to the same project folder, then bring the reply back.

I asked for an outside-agent opinion and received a response back in my main agent app.

docs.title: 4. Choose who takes part
docs.text:
The first page’s council uses three subagents of the same AI. Once you have connected other models, I would start with one fresh agent from each:

  • Two connected AIs: one fresh agent from each. Claude and Codex are one possible pair.
  • Claude, Codex, and Gemini: one fresh agent from each. This is my usual preference.

Once I switch to fresh agents from different AIs, I find the personas and narrow assignments less relevant. A generalist from each app, independently working on the same task, gets pretty good results. Each gets the same brief and relevant material, then a separate fresh synthesis agent brings their findings together.

I've decided who my new council will be.

docs.title: 5. Edit your skills to use your new default council
docs.text:
Tell your main agent which panel you want in both skills. For my usual council:

Edit my /council and /adversarial-review skills to use one fresh Claude agent, one fresh Codex agent, and one fresh Gemini agent as their default panels. The agent should call and retrieve the other two automatically. Give these generalists the same task and relevant material, have them work independently, then use a separate fresh synthesis agent. Keep the existing persona assignments for same-AI panels. Nothing else about either skill should change.

Check that my installed skills and connections support this. Save a lasting personal default that survives plugin updates, show me where it lives and how to undo it, and tell me if a requested model is unavailable rather than silently substituting another.

For a two-model council, name just the two you connected. You can still ask for a different panel on a particular task.

Then open a new session in the same project and ask:

/council Run a small test case by asking each agent what model they are. For this test only, skip the synthesis report and report each agent's response. Also show the model reported by each connection, when available, separately from the agent's own answer.

This checks that the agents respond. Their self-descriptions are not proof of model identity. Use the connection's model information to check that. Ask the main agent to test the saved /adversarial-review panel in the same way.

Once the tests work, use /council to tackle a task and /adversarial-review to examine the draft without spelling out the panel every time. You still supply the goal, files, constraints, and your judgment. After review, apply the useful findings and check the revised work, just as on the first page.

My new council is up and running properly.

docs.title: When a connection stops working
docs.text:
Unfortunately, in my experience, these skills and connections need a little maintenance. AI companies keep changing their apps and models, so a connection will periodically fail. The council skill should tell you when it could not call another agent. When that happens, ask your main AI to use a council of the agents that still work to diagnose and fix it.

Check the login first. Often, you just need to sign in again. Your main AI may not be able to complete the other app’s login for you; it should point you to the app or sign-in window where you can re-verify it.

Usually, you can ask something as simple as:

Use a council to diagnose why my cross-app connections aren’t working and help me fix them. I need you to fix the connection to [other app] so that you can call its agents and retrieve their responses. Use whichever agents are still available. Smoke-test the reconnection by sending a small request and checking that the answer comes back here. Tell me if I need to sign in again myself.

docs.title: Are you taking advantage of AI-driven research?
docs.text:
← Back to the next-steps checklist

Before I decide what to do, I often need to know what other people have tried. What worked? What didn’t? How much applies to my problem? I ask AI to investigate, then bring the findings to a council to help work out what to do with them.

There are two ways I do this. /research-council is a council with a specific job: search the web, read original sources, and compare the evidence. /deep-research asks ChatGPT and Gemini’s dedicated Deep Research tools to produce reports. In either case, I make the request from my project and the agent brings the findings back there. You can choose one route; you don’t need to run both.

docs.title: 1. Choose how to investigate
docs.text:
Skill When to use it Multi-agent research: /research-council Ask your connected AIs to investigate independently, read original sources, and compare what they find. Browser Deep Research: /deep-research Commission reports from ChatGPT and Gemini’s Deep Research tools. Your agent runs them in the browser and brings the reports back to your project.

Which would I use? I usually find browser Deep Research more thorough. I use Research Council for a narrower question, or when I want to save my limited Deep Research requests for a bigger investigation. Research Council still uses the allowances of the AIs doing the work.

docs.title: Multi-agent research
docs.text:
The researchers look for evidence that challenges the answer as well as supports it. A fresh agent brings their reports together. Your working council can then use that evidence to develop a proposal or plan.

/research-council uses the AIs you have connected: one fresh researcher from each available Claude, Codex and Gemini. If you’ve set up multiple AIs for /council or /ask-agents, it uses those same connections.

Grok joins when you ask for it. I find it especially useful for searching X/Twitter, where people discuss new tools and approaches long before there is much written elsewhere. These very AI workflows are a good example.

docs.title: Browser Deep Research
docs.text:
/deep-research uses ChatGPT and Gemini by default. You can ask for just one. The agent operates their Deep Research tools in your browser, so you need access to those products. A Codex or Antigravity connection alone doesn’t provide it.

Not every question needs Deep Research. Requests in both ChatGPT and Gemini are limited. I’ve kept the skills separate because I don’t want to use that allowance every time I ask for a web search.

As of November 2026, OpenAI has announced a shared, token-based usage allowance for ChatGPT and Codex starting in December. That is a change to the overall allowance, not an announced price per Deep Research report. Check your account’s usage limits when choosing how much research to run.

Be careful: Claude offers another skill with the same name

My Claude setup also has /anthropic-skills:deep-research. That skill sends Claude subagents to investigate different parts of a question. It doesn't run ChatGPT or Gemini’s browser tools. If you ask for our /deep-research skill, make clear that you mean the browser workflow from this site.

I’ve chosen how I want to run the research.

docs.title: 2. Ask your AI to set it up
docs.text:
Open a session in your project and ask your agent to install the skill you've chosen. Both are in the GitHub skills folder, separate from the starter kit.

For multi-agent research:

Find and install the research-council skill from the chrisblattman/claudeblattman GitHub repository. Install the entire folder, including its supporting files and SKILL.md, where I keep my other skills. If I already have it, preserve my customizations.

Check which AIs I already have connected and help me set up any others I want to use. Don't start the research yet.

You can start with the AI you already use. If you already run a council with multiple AIs, this skill uses those same connections. Otherwise, the connection walkthrough explains how to add them.

For browser Deep Research:

The setup below uses your agent’s Chrome extension. If your workplace blocks it, you can run Deep Research yourself in an approved browser if your account allows it. Research Council is another option if your workplace allows agent-based research.

Find and install the deep-research skill from the chrisblattman/claudeblattman GitHub repository. I mean the browser workflow that uses ChatGPT and Gemini's Deep Research tools. Install the entire folder, including its supporting files and SKILL.md, where I keep my other skills. If I already have it, preserve my customizations.

Run /deep-research setup. Help me connect your Chrome extension and sign in to the research tools I want to use. Check that you can open Deep Research and enter a prompt, without submitting a research request.

The agent walks you through connecting the Chrome extension and signing in to ChatGPT and Gemini. You can keep your usual browser for everyday work and use Chrome for this. Setup saves what it needs for the next run; the checks don't submit research or use your allowance.

After installing either skill, start a new session in your project so it is available there. To recheck the browser setup later, ask for /deep-research setup.

The research skill I've chosen is ready, and I’ve started a new session.

docs.title: 3. Tell it what you need to learn
docs.text:
Tell it what you are trying to decide, what you already know, and what worries you. I dictate this because I give much more context when I don’t have to type it all out. The agent turns the request into a brief for the researchers.

Like /council, both skills can use /prompt (bundled in the starter kit) behind the scenes when the question needs more preparation. You don’t need to run it separately. If you already have a research prompt, they use it as written unless you ask for changes.

For example:

/research-council I’m interested in the easiest way to measure respondents’ networks because I’m worried about spillover effects in our study. Read the study design and draft questionnaire in this project.

I care about ease for the respondent: this is an online survey, and I don’t want extra questions to discourage people from finishing. I imagine most of the relevant connections will be within [the group or community we’re studying], but I’m not sure how much that assumption matters.

What approaches have other studies used? Compare how much effort they ask of respondents and what they let us learn about possible spillovers. Help me decide what’s worth including in our survey.

To use ChatGPT and Gemini’s Deep Research, start the same request with /deep-research. You can leave out either one:

/deep-research [Insert the same dictated message about the question and context.] Skip Gemini for this run.
Where do the chats and reports go?

The browser skill files its chats in a Deep Research project in ChatGPT and a Deep Research notebook in Gemini. It finds or creates them and tells you if filing is blocked.

Both skills save the question, individual reports and combined findings in your working project. The browser skill keeps the original exports too. Ask the agent to show you where it saved them.

For Gemini, the agent exports the report to a Google Doc, downloads that document to your project folder, and checks that the complete report and its sources are there. Claude then moves the temporary Google Doc to Trash; Codex leaves it in Drive and tells you it can be deleted separately. This is cumbersome, but I find it to be the best way to automate exports from Gemini.

If a browser session or download is interrupted, ask the agent to resume the existing research. It should recover the same report rather than start the question over.

I’ve asked a research question that will help with my work.

docs.title: 4. Read the answer and follow up
docs.text:
When the reports come back, a fresh agent brings them together. You get an answer, the disagreements and gaps that matter, and links to the reports and sources. With one report, you get that report and a short summary. This is part of the skill; there’s no separate step to arrange.

I want the synthesis to explain why a finding deserves weight. It shouldn’t count votes or assume a Deep Research report is better. Three reports citing the same study are still drawing on one study.

Start with the synthesis, then ask about anything that would change your decision. For the network questions:

Which of these approaches has actually been used in an online survey? What do we know about completion rates and how long the questions take? If we ask fewer questions, what would we lose in our ability to measure possible spillovers?

Follow up on the claims that matter for your decision, and open the sources when you need a closer look. If the answer is hard to follow, ask for an explanation. If it misses the point, tell it. The first report gives you something to work with.

Can I combine agent research and Deep Research?

Yes, but ask for both explicitly. Neither skill automatically adds the other. For example:

Use /research-council and /deep-research to investigate the same question independently. Start both, then combine their completed reports into one final synthesis. Keep the individual reports too.

There is no fixed weighting between the two kinds of report. Ask the synthesizer to compare the evidence, explain disagreements, and identify which findings are useful for your question.

If you already have reports, ask the agent to combine those without starting new research.

I’ve read the findings and followed up on the important questions.

docs.title: 5. Put the findings to work
docs.text:
Use the findings to make the decision that prompted the research. They might change your project description, strengthen a proposal, or help you choose what to test next. For the survey example, I’d ask a council to turn the evidence into a draft:

/council Use the research to propose network questions for our online survey. Keep the burden on respondents low, and explain what we can and can’t learn about spillovers with your proposed questions. What should we test before adding them to the survey?

Add your judgment, revise, and use /adversarial-review when you want a fresh examination of the result. For a smaller change, just ask your main agent to apply what you learned.

When you finish, use /done to save where you got to, what the research changed, and what remains open. The reports stay with the project so you can return to them in the next session.

I’ve used the research to move my work forward.

docs.title: Clean up your email backlog
docs.text:
One of the best things AI has done for me is help me manage my email and keep track of what I owe people. But to make that work well, I first had to clean out my existing backlog. That did two things: it cleared the inbox for the first time in years, and it helped me teach the agent the categories and rules I now use to handle new mail.

I started with about 5,000 unread emails. This was partly because I used unread email like a to-do list. If I owed someone a reply or needed to do something, I left the message unread until I got around to it. The backlog was a constant low-grade source of stress. Somewhere in there were things I still needed to do.

This page walks through choosing your buckets, creating filters, and applying those decisions to old mail. Part 2 covers the recurring routine: working through new messages, replying, and correcting the system as you use it.

docs.title: How the pieces work together
docs.text:
I use Gmail. The buckets are labels, which work like tags: a message can have more than one. Applying a label categorizes the message. Archiving it takes it out of the inbox, but you can still find it under its label or in search. Google's label guide explains how to create and manage them.

A filter is a rule Gmail follows when mail arrives. For example, messages from a particular newsletter can get the @ToRead label and skip the inbox. Creating the label alone doesn't create that rule. Several filters can send mail into the same bucket. Google's filter guide shows the settings.

The agent helps you choose these rules and handles messages that need more judgment. “Newsletters from this address go into reading” can be a filter. “This looks like an announcement, but contains a personal request I need to answer” calls for the agent to read the message.

Your agent needs a connection to Gmail that lets it read messages, apply labels, and create filters. Ask it to help you set that up before starting.

docs.title: 1. Decide where unfinished work will go
docs.text:
Before clearing messages, choose where you'll keep the tasks they contain. If you already use a reminder app or a task list, use that.

I wasn't using Google Tasks or Apple Reminders at all, which in retrospect was a mistake. After researching and testing both, I chose Apple Reminders for the flexibility and Siri integration. The key insight: emails that create to-do items should become reminders, not stay unread.

Choose something with little friction. Markdown checklists can work well if your agent manages the list entirely, but they're less convenient for checking your to-dos on the fly.

Treat replies and other work differently. Keep an email that needs a reply in the inbox until you've answered it. If it asks you to do something elsewhere, such as read a draft or submit a form, create a reminder with a link to the email. Once the reminder is saved, you can file the message. If it needs both a reply and a task, create the reminder and keep the email visible until you've replied.

Open a session with your agent and ask:

I want to clean up the email backlog in [account]. I've been using unread messages to remember things I need to do. I want to keep tasks in [my reminder app or task list], with links back to the emails.

First, check that you can add tasks to [app] with the proper due dates. If that doesn't work, help me get it set up.

docs.title: 2. Have it scan your email and suggest buckets
docs.text:
Have the agent inspect a sample before proposing a system. Include recent and older mail, and both read and unread messages. You want categories that reflect what's actually arriving.

Look through a sample of my email across different senders and dates, including read and unread messages. Show me the main categories you find and a few examples of each. Suggest a small set of labels or folders and explain what you would keep in the inbox.

Ask me about important people and messages I don't want to miss. Walk me through the choices one at a time. Leave the messages unchanged while we work this out.

Start with broad categories. Fewer buckets means fewer distinctions for the agent to get wrong. In my case, I separate things I need to respond to, emails I need to see and be aware of, newsletters, and announcements. I also have categories for emails I don't need to see but will want my agent to retrieve later, like receipts.

Here are the main groups in my setup:

Kind of mail Where it belongs Needs a reply or my judgment Inbox, until handled Something I need to see or know Inbox for my check-in; marked read when summarized, filed when requested Newsletters and longer reading @ToRead Institutional announcements @Announcements School notices @School Family correspondence @Family, with important messages kept visible Receipts and expenses Expenses/, with sublabels for pending, personal, and uncertain expenses Routine automated mail I don't need to see Auto-Archive

I also use @ToDo and @ToSelf for messages I flag myself. You don't need all of these labels. Start with the distinctions that matter to you.

React to the examples in ordinary language: “Keep messages from this person in my inbox.” “Put these newsletters together so I can read them later.” “Receipts can be filed, but I need to see a failed payment.”

docs.title: 3. Create the rules and clear old mail in batches
docs.text:
Start with the categories you can agree on quickly. You don't need to make a separate decision about every old newsletter. Review the proposed rule and some examples:

Let's start with [category] over the past [x months]. Show me how many messages you found, a few examples, and any exceptions that might need my attention. Show me the exact filter rule you'd use for future messages in this category, or explain if it needs the agent's judgment instead.

Give the agent your corrections and exceptions. Once you're happy with the rule, ask it to set it up and apply it to the old messages:

Create the label and filter we've agreed on, including my exceptions, for future incoming mail. If this needs your judgment rather than a Gmail filter, save it as an instruction in my email policy instead.

Apply the agreed policy to this category over the past [x months] using our mail connection. Keep read and unread status unchanged. Keep a record of what you changed so we can undo a mistake. Don't delete messages or send replies.

The saved filter handles future mail. Applying the rule to the selected old messages clears that part of the backlog. Make sure the agent tells you which of those it completed, especially if you had to create the filter yourself.

Repeat for each of the suggested categories you're happy with.

docs.title: 4. Find unfinished work and move it to reminders
docs.text:
This is going to take time. It took me about 36 hours to clear my backlog of 5,000 messages. Hopefully most of yours will be easy to archive, especially the old ones. The unresolved requests take more attention. Have the agent read the rest of each conversation before deciding you still owe someone something. You may have answered in a later reply.

I want to get to inbox zero, so let's go through all the remaining email in my inbox, both read and unread, regardless of date. Read the full conversations so you can tell whether a request was already handled.

Show me what can be archived, what needs a reply, what needs another action, and what we're waiting for someone else to do. For each item, give me a link to the email and your suggested next step. Work through them with me until we've dealt with every remaining message.

You can answer: “That's done.” “I still need to read the draft. Add a task for Thursday.” “Draft a reply saying I can meet next week.” Or tell the agent you no longer intend to do something. An old request isn't automatically a current commitment.

Once you've decided what to do, ask:

Save the tasks we've agreed on in [app], with the agreed due dates and links to the original emails. Check that they've appeared there before filing those messages. Keep their read status unchanged.

Leave messages that still need a reply or a decision in my inbox. Save any replies we've drafted without sending them.

docs.title: 5. Check the cleanup and save what you've taught it
docs.text:
Look through a sample of the mail the agent filed. Check the task list as well. The important question is whether you can find the work you still need to do.

My current email skills keep their instructions and records in an exec-assistant/ project folder in Dropbox. Here's the relevant structure. You can put your own folder wherever you keep your AI projects:

exec-assistant/
├── policies/
│   └── email-policy.md       Handling rules, important people, and exceptions
├── config/
│   └── triage-config.md      Label IDs and classification settings
└── state/
    └── triage-run-state.json  Record of mail already processed

Gmail keeps the filters. Your email project folder keeps the instructions the agent follows. Ask it to save what you've decided so the next session can pick up where you left off. The agent maintains the settings and processing records for you.

Ask your agent to adapt this structure to your own setup:

Show me what we've finished, which dates or messages we haven't covered, and what still needs my decision. Give me a sample of the messages you filed so I can check them.

Save our agreed rules in my existing email-assistant folder, or help me create one if I don't have one. Use policies/email-policy.md for handling rules and config/triage-config.md for the labels and settings, unless my installed skills already use different locations. Make sure future sessions and my email skills know where to find them.

Use this email-policy template as a starting point, replacing its defaults with our decisions:
https://github.com/chrisblattman/claudeblattman/blob/main/skills/triage-inbox/assets/email-policy.md

Include our important senders, filters and exceptions, the instruction to preserve read status, and where tasks belong. Tell me where you've saved everything.

Next, put those rules to work on new mail. Recurring email workflows explains how to automate the sorting and, if you want, work through replies and decisions with your agent. These workflows make up my “AI executive assistant” and help me manage my day.

docs.title: Personal life
docs.text:
The same habits that help at work can help with the decisions and paperwork at home. Give the agent the relevant files, explain what matters to you, and work through the choices together.

Workflow What it's for Tax season Organize a complicated tax return, with a detailed case study including what the AI got wrong. Build a personal shopper Collect your requirements and compare options before buying. Vacation planning Keep the plans, preferences, and travel decisions in one place. Health and fitness Bring your records and goals together so the agent has useful context.

Looking for the email guides that used to be here? They're now under Email management. Meeting preparation and follow-up belongs with the project-management guides.

Pick a task you can use this week. You can track it in the everyday work checklist.

docs.title: The council workflow
docs.text:
Start with Council and review: install the skills, develop a task with three independent members, add your judgment, run a fresh four-member review, and revise the work.

The companion guides cover connecting different AI models and changing your defaults, and using deep research to find and assess evidence.

The handoff step covers saving your work for the next session.

docs.title: Recurring email workflows & a daily check-in
docs.text:
I want to spend less time sorting email and more time dealing with the messages that need me. Gmail filters handle the predictable mail. My agent reads what's left and files it using the rules I've taught it. Both put messages into the same buckets, so I can read newsletters, announcements, and receipts together when I need them.

You can stop there and keep answering email in Gmail. I also use /checkin to bring the remaining messages into a conversation with my agent: what I need to know, what needs a reply, and what I need to do.

Before you begin, it will help immensely to spend a few days cleaning up your email backlog and setting filtering rules. That's where you teach the agent what matters to you and decide where unfinished work belongs. This page puts those decisions to work on new mail.

docs.title: 1. Let Gmail and your agent do the sorting
docs.text:
Gmail filters already run without an agent. If I have a filter that sends a newsletter to @ToRead and skips the inbox, Gmail does that when the message arrives. My computer can be off. I don't need /triage-inbox to run that filter again.

But I don't have a Gmail filter for everything. A newsletter might arrive from a new address. The same company might send both a receipt I can file and a failed-payment notice I need to act on. A university email might be a general announcement or a colleague asking me to read a draft. I want the agent to read what's left in the inbox and make those distinctions using the instructions I've given it.

How Gmail filters and inbox triage work together Gmail filters run when mail arrives and file matching messages under Gmail labels. Triage reads the mail left in the inbox against your email policy and uses agent discretion to decide. It files routine mail under those same labels and keeps other messages in the inbox for you to review, in Gmail or with an optional check-in. Matching filing rule Mail left in inbox Routine mail Keep visible Gmail filters On arrival /triage-inbox Reads against your email policy and uses agent discretion to decide Filed under Gmail labels Inbox Ready for your review

Both routes can put mail under the same labels. A newsletter filed by Gmail and one filed by the agent can both end up in @ToRead. The difference is who decides to put it there.

docs.title: What the skill actually does
docs.text:
On each run, /triage-inbox reads the saved policy and checks recent inbox mail, both read and unread. It reads the contents before deciding what to file. Important people, requests, substantive project updates, payment or security problems, and messages I've asked it to hold take priority over a routine filing rule. If it isn't sure, it leaves the message in the inbox for me.

Here are examples of what that means:

What arrives What Gmail has already done What triage adds A regular newsletter covered by a skip-inbox filter Labeled and filed it. Nothing: it's already outside the ordinary inbox review. A reading subscription arrives from a new address that no filter matches Left it in the inbox. Reads it and files it under @ToRead if my saved policy covers it. Otherwise, leaves it for review. A receipt or a failed-payment notice from the same vendor Left it in the inbox because I haven't made a broad sender filter. Files the ordinary receipt under my expense rules; keeps the failed payment visible. A collaborator sends results, with no question and me only CC'd Left it in the inbox. Keeps it visible. No explicit request doesn't mean there's nothing I need to know.

It also checks recent inbox messages that already carry a label I've designated for filing. For example, a filter might have added @ToRead without removing the message from the inbox. If my policy says those messages should be filed, triage can finish that step after checking the contents and exceptions. A label by itself isn't enough reason to archive a message.

docs.title: 2. Install /triage-inbox and connect your rules
docs.text:
The /triage-inbox skill includes its setup templates and supporting files. It is separate from the starter kit. Ask your agent:

Find and install the triage-inbox skill from the chrisblattman/claudeblattman GitHub repository. Install the entire folder, including its assets, references, scripts, and SKILL.md, where I keep my other skills. If I already have it, inspect that copy first and preserve my customizations.

Connect it to the email policy and label settings we saved during cleanup in [my email-assistant folder]. Use our existing mail connection. Keep our labels, exceptions, and read-status choices rather than replacing them with the examples in the skill.

You shouldn't need to recreate the labels or filters. The agent should use the policy and settings you saved on the cleanup page. Have it resolve any missing connection before you run the workflow.

docs.title: 3. Try it and correct the mistakes
docs.text:
/triage-inbox

Look at its report and open a few of the messages it filed. If something went to the wrong place, correct it and have the agent save the exception. To understand a decision, ask:

For the messages you just filed, show me the label you used and which instruction in my email policy supported the decision. Also show me what you left in the inbox because it needed my attention or you weren't sure.

Triage normally looks back from its last successful run, with some overlap to catch missed arrivals. It saves that progress in state/triage-run-state.json inside your email project folder, unless you chose another location during setup. It doesn't clear years of old mail. If you've been away, tell the agent which dates you want covered and have it report any gaps.

The first version will get things wrong. When it does, explain the distinction you want it to learn:

This sender's general announcements can be filed, but a personal request to me needs to stay in the inbox. Move this message back and save that distinction in my email policy for future runs.

Some corrections belong in the agent's policy. Others can become Gmail filters, using the process on the cleanup page. Review the proposed rule and its exceptions before creating it. You don't need a new filter for every unusual email.

docs.title: 4. Put the sorting on a schedule
docs.text:
Once you're happy with the sorting, put it on a schedule. Mine runs automatically at 6 a.m. You can have triage run on your computer or in the cloud. The practical difference is whether your computer needs to be on at 6 a.m.

Where it runs What works well The catch On your computer It can use the skills and email project folder you've already set up. Your computer needs to be awake, online, and running the app when the task starts. In the cloud It can sort your mail while your computer is off. You need to give the cloud task access to your mail and files, and check that the whole skill works there.

A schedule tied to a local project still needs that computer. A cloud schedule uses the files and connections available to the cloud session. The OpenAI scheduling guide and Claude scheduling guide explain the options in each app.

docs.title: Using your Dropbox folders for a cloud run
docs.text:
Dropbox can give the cloud agent access to your current skills and email policy. You need to connect Dropbox to the agent, then tell the scheduled task to read those files each time it runs. Simply putting a folder in Dropbox on your computer doesn't make that connection.

The attraction is that you can keep working in the same folder. Change an email rule, let Dropbox finish syncing, and the next run can fetch the revised file. You shouldn't need to upload it again. If you instead attach a copy of the folder to a chat, you'll need to replace that copy when you make changes.

For example, here's how to prepare this in Claude:

  1. Connect Dropbox. In Claude's desktop app, open Customize → Connectors → Add → Browse connectors, choose Dropbox, and sign in. Dropbox's setup guide also has the web instructions.
  2. Point Claude to your folders. Give it the Dropbox location of the entire /triage-inbox skill folder and your email project folder. Include the supporting files inside the skill folder, not just SKILL.md. Ask it to open your current email policy through the Dropbox connection.
  3. Check the mail connection and the skill. The cloud task needs to be able to read and file Gmail messages. It also needs to run the skill's small programs and save a record of the mail it has handled, so the next run can pick up from there. Dropbox access alone doesn't establish that. Ask the agent to check this in the cloud session before you schedule it.

You can ask:

I want /triage-inbox to run in the cloud while my computer is off. My skill folder is in Dropbox at [folder], and my email project folder is at [folder].

Use the Dropbox connection to read the current skill and email policy at the start of every run. Check that you can access the whole skill folder, run its supporting programs, and use my Gmail connection to read and file messages.

Set up a place to save which messages you've handled so each run can continue from the last one. Make sure this also works with any triage I run myself, including through /checkin if I use it. Tell me if anything still needs my computer to be on.

Test the setup without changing any email. If something needs adapting for cloud use, explain what and help me fix it before we schedule the task.

The skill currently saves its progress in files on a computer. Ask the agent to adapt that part if your cloud app needs a different way to keep track of what it's done.

docs.title: Set the schedule
docs.text:
Once the setup works, ask:

Set up /triage-inbox to run every day at 6 a.m. in [my timezone] for [email account], using the setup we just tested.

Read the current skill and email policy from [folder locations] each time. You can label and file mail under the rules we've agreed on. Don't send replies.

Keep routine runs quiet. Tell me if a run fails or can't read the mail it needs. Show me where I can find and change the schedule.

Check the first run. If you chose the cloud, make sure it worked with your computer off and read the latest policy. I leave /checkin for when I'm at the computer and ready to answer questions.

docs.title: 5. Optional: work through your email with /checkin
docs.text:
You can keep reading and answering the remaining mail in Gmail. If you'd like your agent to summarize it and help you work through replies and decisions, add /checkin.

When I sit down at my computer at 8 a.m., I run /checkin. I may run it three to five times a day. Each time, it automatically invokes /triage-inbox to catch mail that arrived since the last run. Scheduling triage at 6 a.m. just helps me start the day a little quicker on that first check-in.

Install it and choose your preferences:

Find and install the checkin skill from the chrisblattman/claudeblattman GitHub repository. Install the entire folder, including its assets, references, scripts, and SKILL.md, where I keep my other skills. If I already have it, inspect that copy first and preserve my customizations.

Use the same email policy, label settings, and mail connection as /triage-inbox in [my email-assistant folder], along with my task app. Keep our existing choices.

Walk me through the check-in preferences, including marking FYIs read, important personal labels, quarantine digests, newsletter reading holds, and whether you will send approved replies or just prepare drafts. Save our choices so I don't have to repeat them.

The skill starts with email. Calendar review and meeting preparation are options you can ask for separately.

docs.title: Work through the messages
docs.text:
Once setup is done, ask:

/checkin

My check-in gives me two groups:

  • FYIs: things I need to know. The agent reads the message and its context, marks it read, and tells me the substance. If someone confirms that a document arrived, I usually just need to know that. This is for messages that need no action from me. An attachment I still need to read belongs in the next group.
  • Things that need my attention. Show me what the person wants, link to the message, and suggest the next step. That might be a reply, a decision, or work I need to do elsewhere.

The agent explains this FYI behavior during setup and saves your preference. If you want those messages left unread, tell it. Showing me an FYI doesn't archive it. It stays in the inbox unless I ask to file it or have a separate rule for that. Once I've read the summaries, I can say:

Archive the FYIs you just showed me.

Work through a manageable batch at a time. You can respond in ordinary language:

For the first email, draft a reply saying Tuesday works for me. Show me the draft before sending it.

For the second, I need to read the attachment before replying. Add a reminder for Thursday with a link to the email.

Leave the third for now. I haven't decided yet.

The distinction from cleanup still matters: a message needing a reply stays visible until you've handled it. Work outside email goes into the task app you chose, with a link back to the message. Creating a reminder doesn't automatically archive the email. If the reminder is now where you'll track the work, ask for both:

Add this task to [my task app], with the agreed due date and a link to the email. Check that the reminder was saved correctly, then archive the email.

Have the agent check the thread before telling you something is overdue. You may already have replied, or the person may have withdrawn the request.

If its drafts don't sound like you, give it a few emails you've written and explain what you'd change. The email voice template gives you a place to save those preferences.

Ask for the next batch when you're ready. The agent saves your decisions and unfinished drafts as you go. If you stop halfway through, use /checkin resume to pick up where you left off.

docs.title: Adjust the extra checks
docs.text:
My setup also checks important personal mail and quarantine digests, and gives some newsletters time to sit unread. During setup, the agent will ask which labels, digests, and subscriptions you use. You can keep these checks, adapt them, or turn them off:

Don't need a separate family review?

This check looks through the family or other important personal labels you choose, including older unread mail that might have been filed out of the inbox. If you don't need a separate pass:

Turn off the separate family-label review in /checkin from now on and save that preference. Keep reviewing family messages that appear in my ordinary inbox.
Don't need quarantine review?

Some employers and universities block suspicious mail before it reaches your inbox, then send a digest of what they held. This check reads your provider's digest and flags messages you may want to recover. It doesn't release messages or change your spam protection. If you don't receive these digests:

Turn off quarantine review in /checkin from now on and save that preference.
Change the newsletter reading window

A reading hold gives me time to read a newsletter myself. My filters and triage file reading subscriptions under @ToRead, out of the inbox, while leaving them unread. For selected newsletters, I protect that unread status for 48 hours after each edition arrives.

The current hold is a minimum reading window, not a timer that clears the message at hour 48. After the window ends, the agent can mark an edition read if it reviews it and finds nothing I still need to do or read. A filed newsletter isn't automatically pulled back into check-in just because the hold expired.

You can choose your subscriptions and change the period:

Give [newsletter names] a 72-hour reading hold instead of 48 hours. Keep filing them under my reading label, but leave each edition unread during that window. Save this preference for /triage-inbox and /checkin.

Or turn off the special hold:

Turn off newsletter-specific reading windows in /checkin and /triage-inbox from now on and save that preference. Keep any messages I've explicitly asked you to leave unread.

You can turn any of these back on by asking the agent and telling it to save the change.

docs.title: 6. Add a digest for mail you read together
docs.text:
Once your mail is being filed into useful groups, consider building a digest for messages you'd rather read together. You can do this whether or not you use /checkin. The labels and filters you created during email cleanup give these skills a specific set of messages to read together.

My school-email digest runs twice a week. Gmail rules file school mail under @School, out of the inbox. The digest reads the messages collected there since the previous digest, extracts deadlines, schedule changes, and things we need to do, and emails me a summary. Once the digest sends successfully, the skill marks the processed messages read and keeps their @School label. I can read one digest instead of opening each school email separately. The school-digest walkthrough shows how to build and calibrate your own, using a synthetic family example.

You could also build meeting preparation and follow-up around correspondence with your team: collect the decisions and open questions before a meeting, then use the discussion afterward to update the tasks and follow-ups. The useful starting point is a group of emails you keep reviewing for the same purpose.

docs.title: Prepare for and follow up on meetings
docs.text:
Meeting skills are being updated

We’re updating the pre- and post-meeting skills to work with the project setup described on this site. You can use the prompts below now; the reusable skills are being refreshed.

I use these skills to get a brief before a meeting and a summary afterward, right in the conversation with my agent. I often also use them to prepare pre- or post-meeting emails to my team.

/pre-meeting prepares you for the conversation. It reads the project description, dashboard, previous meeting records and recent correspondence. You get a brief on what's happened, what's unfinished and what needs a decision, followed by a draft agenda email.

/post-meeting helps you make sense of what happened. It reads the transcript and gives you a summary of the discussion, decisions, action items and open questions, followed by a draft follow-up email for the team.

Both show their results in the agent chat. Add nosend if you want only the brief or summary, without an email draft. Both draft first and send only when you ask. Review the draft, then say “send” if you want the agent to send it. You can also ask it to save the draft in your mailbox and send it yourself.

Prepare, meet, follow up Pre-meeting produces a brief in your agent chat; post-meeting produces a summary. Downward arrows show the separate agenda and follow-up email drafts. You can save these in your mailbox or explicitly ask the agent to send them. With nosend, skip the email drafts. /pre-meeting Brief in your chat Have the meeting Capture a transcript /post-meeting Summary in your chat Agenda email draft Unsent until you ask Follow-up email draft Unsent until you ask Draft first. Send only when you ask. How this fits with weekly review, the project description and dashboard

/weekly-review brings the project record up to date. It reads meeting transcripts alongside your comments, correspondence and other project material. It updates the dashboard and dated history, and proposes changes to the project description for you to approve. This workflow is explained in Refresh your project dashboard and description.

Meetings and the continuing project record An updated project description and dashboard inform the pre-meeting brief. Post-meeting and weekly-review are optional. Weekly-review can read the transcript and corrections directly without a post-meeting summary. Its updates to the project record inform the next brief. Updated project documents inform the next brief Project description + dashboard /pre-meeting Prepare Meeting + transcript /post-meeting Optional summary /weekly-review Optional refresh Transcript + comments; no summary required Refresh dashboard; approve project-description changes separately

The meeting skills prepare an account for you and your team. Weekly review maintains the continuing project record. It can read the transcript directly; a post-meeting summary is optional. The updated project description and dashboard then give the next pre-meeting brief its starting point.

docs.title: 1. Install the skills
docs.text:
Ask your agent to install /pre-meeting and /post-meeting:

Install the pre-meeting and post-meeting skills from the chrisblattman/claudeblattman GitHub repository for this app. If they're already installed, update them while preserving my customizations. If I have pre-meeting-brief, replace it with pre-meeting and keep my customizations.

When you name a project, the skills find its folder and read PROJECT_CONFIG.json. The project setup guide walks you through creating this file. It records where to find your project documents and transcripts, along with the email addresses, project keywords and WhatsApp chats to check for correspondence. Set those sources up once and both meeting skills can reuse them. Connect the apps your project uses once, too; recording their locations in the file doesn't connect an account by itself.

docs.title: 2. Prepare a brief
docs.text:
Open a session with your agent and name the project:

/pre-meeting Prepare for this morning's [project] meeting.

The skill reads the project description and dashboard, including your comments, then checks previous meetings and recent correspondence. It looks in the project's transcript folder, including its archive, and uses your connected transcription app when a record is missing locally.

For recent correspondence, it starts from your last successful project review, or the latest saved weekly review. If neither exists, it looks back 14 days. You can choose a different starting date with since:2026-11-01. The brief tells you which dates it covered. Older transcripts still matter when they explain an outstanding decision or the latest review; there isn't a separate meeting-skill log that marks them as finished.

You get the brief followed by a draft agenda email, with the From, To and any Cc/Bcc addresses shown. If an address is missing, the agent flags it rather than guessing. The draft appears in the chat. You can say “send” to have the agent send that email, or ask it to save the draft in your mailbox and send it yourself. Saving a draft does not deliver it to anyone.

If your account has disabled sending emails

The skill can still save the email in your mailbox if your account allows draft creation. Open your mail app, look in Drafts, and send it from there. The agent tells you when the draft is saved. If your account also blocks creating drafts, the skill gives you the email text to copy into a new message.

A few options you can add:

  • nosend: just the brief, without an email draft.
  • light or full: a shorter or more detailed brief. Even when I only want a quick catch-up, I want the agent to read the project description and dashboard so it understands what we're trying to do and where things stand. The longer version spends more time on correspondence, previous meetings and what each person needs to prepare.
  • save: also save the brief in the project folder. Combine it with nosend if you want to keep the brief without drafting email.

docs.title: 3. Capture the discussion and leave your own notes
docs.text:
I like Granola right now (as of November 2026) because I can organize my meetings into project folders within the app. Another transcription app works too, as long as its connector lets your agent read the transcripts.

I also leave comments in the dashboard while we're meeting: what's been handled, what the next open question is, or which table I want to see next time. The transcript records the discussion. My comments tell the agent what I want it to do with it. Both inform the post-meeting summary.

docs.title: 4. Write the summary
docs.text:
/post-meeting Summarize this morning's [project] meeting.

The skill finds the meeting in your project's transcript folder or fetches it from your connected transcription app. When it fetches a transcript, it saves a text copy in the project's configured transcript folder, with the meeting date and source recorded. It reuses an existing copy rather than creating duplicates. If it can't read the transcript or save the file, it tells you what is missing.

You get the discussion, decisions, action items and unresolved questions in the chat, followed by an email draft with its sender and recipients shown. Check the decisions as well as the tasks. “We discussed moving the deadline” is different from “we moved the deadline.” Correct the account before sharing it.

Options you can add:

  • nosend: just the summary, without an email draft.
  • save: also save the summary in the project folder. nosend save saves it without drafting email.

Keep the transcripts in the project folder even if you save a summary. Future work may need reasoning that didn't make it into the summary.

docs.title: 5. Bring the decisions back into the project
docs.text:
I don't run /post-meeting after every meeting. The larger the team and the more decisions we made, the more likely I am to use it and send a summary email. For a lot of other work, I skip straight to /weekly-review to keep the project record up to date. It can read the transcript and my dashboard comments without a post-meeting summary:

/weekly-review [project name]

If the summary gets something wrong, tell the agent the correction. To keep it for future reviews, also put it in the dashboard's Human notes / corrections area, or ask: “Add this to my dashboard notes for today's meeting: Friday was suggested as a deadline, but we didn't agree to it.” The agent should confirm where it saved the note. If it can't edit the dashboard, paste the note there yourself. That gives the next review a saved correction to read, even if it starts in a different chat.

Read the guide to refreshing your project dashboard and description for more detail.

docs.title: Set up a project for AI collaboration
docs.text:
Your agent works better when it knows where to find things. I try to give my projects a consistent folder structure, whether I'm working on research, a personal project, or my AI setup. Background research goes in a predictable place. So do drafts, meeting transcripts, and the results of councils and reviews. That saves me from explaining where to look and where to put the next file every time I start a session.

When I start a project, I initialize a few of those folders, even if they're empty. I don't need the whole structure on day one. Some skills create their own folders when I first use them. But choosing a few destinations early helps keep the project organized before it gets out of hand.

I use Dropbox, but the same approach works with OneDrive, Box, or folders stored locally on your computer. Use the storage you and your collaborators already work with.

Already have a project folder, but it's a mess? Start with Clean up an existing project.

docs.title: What a structured project looks like
docs.text:
Here is a starting point. You can change the names. The useful part is knowing what belongs where.

My project/
├── PROJECT_INDEX.md       Where material lives and which versions are current
├── PROJECT_STATUS.md      Current overview and next actions
├── AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md  Standing instructions for the agents you use
├── research/              Background research, reports, and source notes
├── council/               Prompts, independent reports, and synthesis
├── drafts/                The work you are developing
└── transcripts/           Project meeting transcripts

You might start with drafts/ and research/, and add transcripts/ if the project involves meetings. A folder for council runs can wait until your first run. The index can also point to material elsewhere: a shared Google Doc, a team's data folder, or a code repository on GitHub. They don't all have to move into this folder.

A research project might look like this, with the AI work collected under 10_AI_Collaboration/:

Research project/
├── 01_Paper/
├── 02_Presentations/
├── 03_Literature/
├── 04_Referee_Reports/
├── 05_Submissions/
├── 06_IRB/
├── 10_AI_Collaboration/
│   ├── PROJECT_INDEX.md
│   ├── TODO.md
│   ├── research/
│   ├── council/
│   ├── Transcripts/
│   ├── Weekly_Reviews/
│   └── Dashboard_Archive/
└── …                      Other project folders as needed

Use the parts that fit your project. A paper might need referee reports and submissions but no IRB folder. Data, code, and fieldwork material can stay in the locations your team already uses. The numbers aren't important enough to rename a shared folder that already works.

The structure becomes useful when your skills follow it:

  • Research: use research/ for reports from /research-council and /deep-research. In the research-project example above, that means 10_AI_Collaboration/research/. Have the setup agent check where your installed skills save their work and adjust their destinations to match.
  • Councils and reviews: /council and /adversarial-review save the prompt, reports, and synthesis together. For a research project, I'd put these in 10_AI_Collaboration/council/ and save that choice in the project's CLAUDE.md and, if you use Codex, AGENTS.md. Then you don't have to repeat the destination every time. A project instruction can say: “Save /council and /adversarial-review runs in dated folders under 10_AI_Collaboration/council/, relative to this project's root.”
  • Meetings: I have a script that maps Granola folders to project folders and files transcripts there. You can set up transcript filing and later schedule it. You'll choose the transcript destination during project setup, and then set up the recurring task separately.

Setting this up will help you and your agents find past work, and give your skills a consistent place to save new work.

Next: Build a project dashboard if you want a shared view of the project's progress and decisions.

docs.title: 1. Install /setup-project-management
docs.text:
My /setup-project-management skill walks you through choosing a structure and getting the project set up. It's separate from the starter kit. If you haven't installed it, give your agent the link and ask it to install the skill for your app.

I've installed /setup-project-management.

docs.title: 2. Set up your project
docs.text:
Open the project folder in your agent and ask:

Use /setup-project-management to set up this project. My personal projects
might be set up differently than what this skill expects, so please keep
track of our structural choices so that we can tailor this skill to my own
projects when we are done.

Your projects may look different from mine, so expect some back-and-forth the first time. Tell the agent which folders you need, what you call them, and where existing work should stay. Look over its proposed structure together before it creates anything.

The project has the folders I want, and its instructions say where each skill should save its work.

docs.title: 3. Adapt the skill for your next project
docs.text:
Once you've worked through the first setup, use those choices to improve your own copy of /setup-project-management. You shouldn't have to explain the same folder preferences again next time.

Now help me adapt my copy of /setup-project-management using the structural
choices we made. Make my folder names and output destinations the defaults
for future projects, with options for different kinds of projects. Keep this
project's people, current status, and one-off decisions out of the skill.
Show me what you changed.

I've adapted the skill to my preferences, or kept its defaults because they fit.

docs.title: Create your project description and dashboard
docs.text:
Project management skills are being updated

We’re updating the project setup skill to work with the project description and dashboard described on this site. You can use the prompts below now; the reusable skill is being refreshed.

Every project should have a document that says what you're trying to do, how you plan to do it, and why. I think of this as its ground truth: the account you've agreed on and keep updating as the work changes. Alongside it, I want a dashboard that tells me where things stand and what needs my attention.

I use these documents for three jobs:

  • Keep the project moving. See what's on my plate, what my collaborators are doing, and what needs a decision.
  • Write about the project. Start a proposal, report, or IRB application with the substance already in one place.
  • Prepare for meetings and follow up. Come in prepped, remember what we said we'd do, and leave with a record of what we decided.

I've settled on using two tabs in a Google Doc. Tab 1 is the dashboard and meeting log. Tab 2 is the project description. In my research projects, I call it the research design: the big questions, the literature we're building on, and the details of how we'll answer them. For another kind of project, it might be a plan for a training program or a new service.

Tab 1 works better when it has Tab 2 to guide it. The description tells the agent what matters, so it can do more than summarize whatever came up in the last meeting.

I like Google Docs because it's easy to share with my team, I can use visual cues like green, yellow, and red lights, and I can talk to my agent by leaving comments. You can use local Markdown files instead, or another document type your team already maintains. The useful part is having an agreed account of the project that both people and agents can find.

docs.title: 1. Start with the project description
docs.text:
Start with what you already have: a proposal, a brief, or notes from the discussions that got the project going. You can try this before setting up the folders or installing a skill:

Read [proposal, brief, or project notes]. Help me turn this into a current description of the project: what we're trying to do, how we plan to do it, and the decisions we've made. Show me what's missing or contradictory, and work through those questions with me.

For a research project, I'd want the description to explain the main hypothesis, why this is an innovation, and how we plan to test it. Include the practical details too: the intervention, sample, measures, and analysis. The example below is a simpler project plan for a training-program pilot. A research design would need those additional details.

Example: Tab 2 — the project plan

This is Tab 2 for a fictional training-program pilot. All names, dates, and facts are invented. It illustrates a project plan, not a validated research protocol.

Last reviewed: June 10, 2026.

Question and purpose

Can the team deliver a short workshop and collect useful participant feedback before investing in a larger program?

Current approach

Run a small feasibility pilot. Observe delivery problems, collect feedback, and record which parts need revision. The pilot is intended to improve the program and the team's procedures; it is not designed to establish a causal effect on participants' later outcomes.

What we need to learn

  • Can the workshop fit the available time?
  • Which instructions are confusing?
  • Can the team administer the short feedback survey consistently?
  • What would need to change before expansion?

Decisions and rationale

Date Accepted decision Reason and source June 3 Start with a pilot before expanding. Test delivery with limited resources; initial project plan. June 10 Shorten the pilot and revise the survey accordingly. Planning discussion identified timing constraints; June 10 meeting note.

Open design questions

The final survey items and criteria for expansion remain to be agreed. Keep those as questions rather than filling them with AI-generated decisions.

Change log

June 10: Recorded the accepted shorter-pilot scope and the survey implication. The proposed venue date and corrected participant count remain operational details in Tab 1.

A routine dashboard refresh should identify a relevant plan change and propose it here. It should not overwrite this tab with a fresh reconstruction every week.

The bulk of this work is likely to be more human than agent driven, but that's part of the point. It's a helpful commitment device: writing the design forces me to think strategically about the project.

I think about three kinds of projects:

  • New projects, where we're writing the first proposals. There may be little to collect yet. Work through the big questions with the agent and use the design document to record where you land. This is where I've seen a big payoff: the thinking you do here feeds the first proposals and gives later AI work something to build on.
  • Projects in flux. Meetings and new drafts may have moved the project beyond the old design. Have the agent compare them and show you what has changed. Spend your time on the unresolved choices and update the design as you settle them.
  • Projects that haven't changed much. Some updates are mechanical: another cohort, revised numbers, a completed stage. Then take a strategic look. Does the current paper or proposal explain the project better than the old design document? Bring that thinking back into the design so the next draft starts from it.

I'd revisit the research design roughly every six months for an established project, but potentially every other week for a nascent one. A new proposal or a substantial change is another reason to return to it. The dashboard (Tab 1) changes more often, ideally after every meeting.

docs.title: 2. Install /setup-project-management
docs.text:
My /setup-project-management skill can help you put this together. If you used it to organize the project folder, you already have it.

Need to install the skill?

Ask your agent:

Find and install the setup-project-management skill from the claudeblattman GitHub repository. Install the entire folder, containing any references, templates, and the SKILL.md file. Put it where I store all my other skills.

docs.title: 3. Build the two tabs with your agent
docs.text:
Open a session in your project. Ask for help building the first iteration of the project or research design document. Working in the project will guide your agent on what resources and documents to draw from, including your meeting transcripts. You can also point it to early emails where you worked out what the project was for.

Adding dashboard to /setup-project-management tells the agent you want help creating or editing Tab 1 or Tab 2, without going through the full project-folder setup (assuming you've already set this up).

/setup-project-management dashboard

Help me build a project description and dashboard for this project. Read the material in [project folder] and these other sources: [links or locations]. The project is [new / changing substantially / fairly stable].

Start with Tab 2, the project description. Use what we've already written and our meeting discussions to explain what we're trying to do, our approach, and the decisions behind it. For a research project, include the big question, the literature we're building on, why this is an innovation, and the details of the research design. Show me where our recent discussions or drafts differ from the existing plan. Work through the important gaps and decisions with me.

Then draft Tab 1, Overview & Meeting Log. Use the design to help identify our priorities, decisions needed, and next actions. Keep a dated history of meetings and changes below the current dashboard, and leave a place for our notes and corrections.

Use [existing Google Doc link / a new Google Doc / local files in this folder]. Link to the sources so we can check it. Add the [Google Doc] link to PROJECT_INDEX.md so we always know where to find the dashboard.

The agent should walk you through the missing pieces. For a new project, expect more back-and-forth about the design. You'll likely need to write the majority of the document by hand.

Example: Tab 1 — the dashboard and meeting log

This is Tab 1 for the same fictional Riverside training pilot. It shows what the team needs to do now and keeps a dated record of what changed.

Current dashboard

=== PROJECT STATUS DASHBOARD ===

Project: Riverside training pilot

Stage: Middle — preparing the pilot

Last successful refresh: June 10, 2026

Evidence checked: June 10 planning note; current project plan; team correction.

Objective: Test whether a short workshop is feasible before deciding whether to expand it.

Priority Current status Next action Confirm the venue June 12 is unavailable. June 19 is proposed, not confirmed. Coordinator to confirm availability; deadline not yet agreed. Prepare the participant survey The team accepted a shorter pilot and needs a matching survey. Revise the survey; owner to confirm. Check the participant list Team correction: 36 participants, replacing the earlier count of 40. Use the corrected count; keep the correction in the history.

Decision needed: Confirm the date before invitations go out.

Plan change: The shorter pilot has been accepted. The corresponding change in Tab 2 is recorded separately with its rationale.

Source coverage: Selected local notes and the project plan. Email and calendar were not searched, so this dashboard does not independently verify venue availability.

=== DASHBOARD END ===

Human notes and corrections

This area stays outside the replaced dashboard. A teammate can add a correction here or edit the dashboard directly; the next refresh must read both.

June 10: The current participant count is 36. The previous list included four people who withdrew.

=== WEEKLY SUMMARIES START ===

June 10 update

Review ID: riverside-2026-06-10-planning-note

Changes: June 12 marked unavailable; June 19 retained as a proposal. Participant count corrected. Shorter-pilot decision recorded, with the matching plan change tracked in Tab 2. Survey revision has no assigned owner yet.

Sources: meetings/2026-06-10.md; team correction in this Doc; drafts/project-plan.md. These are illustrative paths, not downloadable source files.

June 3 update

Changes: June 12 was the provisional workshop date; the working participant count was 40. Venue confirmation and survey preparation remained open.

What the next refresh should do

Preserve the corrected count and outstanding actions unless new evidence supersedes them. Keep the June 19 date provisional until confirmed. Retain both dated entries, and avoid duplicating the June 10 entry on a retry. Update the research plan only when a substantive change has been agreed.

docs.title: 4. Iterate and rewrite the project description
docs.text:
Spend time getting Tab 2 right. Read the draft, rewrite the argument, and work through the gaps. The agent can help organize the material and identify inconsistencies, but you need to decide what you're trying to learn, how you'll learn it, and what story you want to present.

This document feeds into so many of my proposals and reports that spending a few hours getting it right pays off quickly. By the time I've sent off two proposals, or even one proposal and the IRB application, I've already reused that work.

Once you've revised the design, ask the agent to check whether Tab 1 needs any changes. Usually it shouldn't change much. Rewriting the argument in Tab 2 doesn't necessarily change the tasks or decisions on the dashboard.

Make any revisions to Tab 1 as needed based on my revisions to Tab 2.

docs.title: Keep track of progress
docs.text:
After a meeting, I read Tab 1 to see what's on my plate, what's on my collaborators' plates, and whether I'm the bottleneck for anything. It's essentially a to-do list. Correct anything the agent misunderstood, and leave a comment when a task is finished or a priority changes.

Refresh your dashboard explains how to use those comments and the meeting transcript to keep it current. The review also suggests changes to Tab 2 when a decision changes the underlying plan.

docs.title: Write proposals, reports, and IRB applications
docs.text:
Use Tab 2 when you need to write about the project. Give the agent the description and the requirements of the document you're writing. For a progress report, include the dashboard and recent results too. Ask it to identify missing information before drafting. A funder may need a budget or an institution may need details about consent that your description doesn't yet contain.

Use our project description in [document] to help draft [proposal, report, or IRB application]. Read the requirements in [file or link] and any relevant results in [folder].

Show me which parts we can write from this material and what information is still missing. Work through the gaps with me, then draft the document.

The /proposal-write instructions describe a fuller proposal-writing workflow. If the writing helps you explain the project better, bring that thinking back into Tab 2 so the next draft benefits from it.

docs.title: Prepare for the next meeting
docs.text:
