Before the next meeting, I read Tab 1 again. It helps me arrive with the right strategic agenda and remember the tasks I asked people to do. If we're reconsidering the approach, I want Tab 2 in front of us too.

Prepare for and follow up on meetings shows how to ask for a briefing, capture decisions, and draft a follow-up when you need one. Its reusable meeting skills still need setup updates, but you can try the plain-language prompts now with the project material your agent can read.

Next: Refresh your dashboard and project description.

docs.title: Project management
docs.text:
Give the project one home and an account of what you're trying to do. That description gives you and your agent something to draw on when writing a proposal or report, deciding what comes next, or preparing for a meeting. The dashboard keeps the immediate work in view.

Workflow What it's for Set up a project Establish the folders, shared context, and instructions you'll use across sessions. Clean up an existing project Recover useful work and bring scattered files together. Create a project description and dashboard Write the underlying project description and build a dashboard around it. See the project plan example and dashboard example. Refresh the dashboard and description Bring in meeting notes and decisions, update the dashboard, and review suggested changes to the description. Prepare for and follow up on meetings Get ready for a discussion and turn it into decisions and next actions.

Need to investigate a question? See Research. To recover a decision from an old AI conversation, see Find past work.

Track what you've tried in the project section of the optional checklist.

docs.title: Find past work with /recall
docs.text:
I kept solving the same problem twice. First because I'd forgotten I'd solved it, second because I couldn't find the session where I did. /recall fixed that.

Recall searches past Claude Code and Codex conversations saved on your computer. You can use it to recover a decision, find a useful answer, or pick up work from an earlier session. It was created by arjunkmrm; I didn't build it.

docs.title: 1. Install the skill
docs.text:
Ask your agent:

Find and install Recall from https://github.com/arjunkmrm/recall. Follow its setup instructions and include the supporting files it needs. Put it where I keep my other skills, then check that it can find my past conversations.

The first search builds a searchable record of your past conversations. If the skill doesn't appear after installation, start a new session.

docs.title: 2. Ask for something you remember working on
docs.text:
You don't need to remember the exact words or which session you used. Give the agent the project name, an approximate date, or a phrase you remember. For example:

Use Recall to find the conversation where we decided which outcomes to measure in [project]. Read the relevant discussion and tell me what we agreed, why, and what we left unresolved.

You can also ask it to find a draft you liked, an approach you tried in another project, or an explanation you want to read again. If the first search misses it, give the agent another clue or ask it to try different terms.

docs.title: 3. Bring the useful work into your project
docs.text:
Once you've found the conversation, ask the agent to compare it with what you're working on now:

Compare what you found with our current project notes. Show me any decisions or useful context we're missing, and flag anything that conflicts with what [Person] and I decided in our meeting this morning.

Give it the meeting transcript or notes so it has that discussion to compare against. Once you've worked through any differences, have it save the decisions you want to keep in the project's documents.

docs.title: 4. Know what it can find
docs.text:
Recall searches conversation files available on the computer running it. If you did the work on another device, you may need to search there. It can't recover a conversation file that is no longer available.

If you've moved your conversation files and searches seem incomplete, ask the agent to refresh Recall's search index and check which files it can see.

Keep important decisions in your project documents even when you use Recall. Finding the old discussion is useful; having the agreed decision ready for the next session is better. Clean up an existing project shows how to bring that scattered work together.

docs.title: Research
docs.text:
Before starting a project or deciding what to do next, I often want to know what other people have already tried. AI can help search for that work, compare the evidence, and find gaps in what we know.

There are two ways I do this:

Approach What it does Multi-agent research Use /research-council to have agents search independently, check their sources, and bring their findings together. Browser Deep Research Use /deep-research to commission reports from ChatGPT and Gemini's dedicated Deep Research tools.

Both links lead into the same research guide, which explains the choices, setup, and how to ask a useful question. Choose the route that fits the work; you don't need to run both.

Save the findings with the project they inform. The project-management guides explain how to keep that evidence alongside the project's description, decisions, and next steps.

docs.title: Create your own email digests
docs.text:
Some emails are easier to read together, either because the latest update replaces what you were told yesterday or because you get so many of them. School notices are a good example, especially with more than one child at more than one school. I want to know about the permission form and the change in pickup time without opening every newsletter.

A digest gives the agent that job. It reads a group of emails and brings you the things you need to act on, upcoming events, and anything else worth knowing. You can use the same approach for announcements from your employer or a professional association.

This builds on the email cleanup workflow. The idea is simple:

Gmail filters or /triage-inbox file messages into a folder → the digest skill periodically reads the new mail in that folder → one digest arrives in your inbox.

The skill checks messages it hasn't processed yet, whether they're read or unread. That way, opening an email yourself doesn't leave it out of the digest.

docs.title: 1. Choose the mail you want to read together
docs.text:
Start with one group of messages. If you already have a label for school notices or announcements, use it. Otherwise, have your agent help you create one using the label and filter instructions.

Keep personal requests and urgent messages visible. You may want the school newsletter in a digest, but a teacher asking to speak with you today deserves your attention sooner.

Your agent needs a connection that can search and read your Gmail. You can ask it to check that connection and find a sample:

I'd like a digest of the emails under [Gmail label]. Check that you can read them, including messages outside my inbox.

Read a sample from the past two weeks. Show me what needs action, what belongs on my calendar, what's useful to know, and what you would leave out. Include links to the emails. Don't change the messages.

docs.title: 2. Teach it what matters to you
docs.text:
The school decides what to send. You decide what matters to your family. The agent needs to learn that distinction from you.

Go through the sample together. A newsletter may be mostly stories you can skip, with an early dismissal notice halfway down. An event marked “IMPORTANT” may be for a grade your child isn't in. Tell the agent why one belongs in the digest and the other doesn't.

Let's work through your choices. Show me a few emails at a time and explain what you would include or skip. Ask me about the ones you're unsure of.

Use my corrections to write rules for future digests. Then try those rules on another group of emails and show me where they don't give you a clear answer.

Save the rules in my email-assistant folder at [location].

Give it the context it needs, such as which grades or programs matter to you. Review some of the emails it would skip, too. Otherwise you'll see the unnecessary items it included and miss the important ones it left out.

docs.title: 3. Keep dates tied to the original email
docs.text:
A wrong deadline can make a digest worse than no digest. Ask the agent to copy the sentence containing the date and put it beside the summary, with a link to the email.

For each deadline or schedule change, include the exact wording from the email and a link to it. If two messages give different dates, flag the conflict. If you can't tell what a date refers to, ask me rather than guessing.

The quote makes a mistake easier to spot. It doesn't guarantee the agent chose the right date or noticed a later correction. Open the original when a deadline matters or something looks wrong.

docs.title: 4. Check the first digest
docs.text:
Here's a shortened, fictional school example. The names, schools, dates, and messages are invented. In your digest, each item should link back to its email.

SCHOOL EMAIL DIGEST
March 1–3

MAYA — LINCOLN PREP

Action needed
• Submit the course selection form by March 10.
  Source: “Course selection forms must be submitted by March 10.”

Coming up
• Parent-teacher conferences: March 13–14. Sign-up is open.
  Sign up: [link from the email]

Worth knowing
• The college counseling series for ninth graders starts in April.

SAM — RIVERSIDE ACADEMY

Action needed
• Return the permission form for the history field trip.
  No deadline given in the email.

Coming up
• Early dismissal on March 7.
  Source: “Students will be dismissed at 12:30 p.m. on March 7.”

Left out: fundraising appeals and repeated event reminders.

Check whether you can tell what you need to do. If “permission form” isn't enough, ask for the form link and who needs to sign it. If an item doesn't matter to you, explain why and have the agent save that correction in the rules.

docs.title: 5. Save it as a skill and choose when to run it
docs.text:
Once you like the result, use the announcement-digest skill as a starting point. It reads labeled mail, applies your saved rules, and keeps a record of the messages it has processed so later digests don't repeat them.

Find and install the announcement-digest skill from the chrisblattman/claudeblattman GitHub repository.

Adapt it to the Gmail label and rules we've just worked out. Keep its rules and record of processed emails in [my email-assistant folder]. Use my existing Gmail connection.

Prepare a digest for me to review, and ask before sending it.

The skill processes all new emails since its last completed run, including any you've already opened yourself. Once the digest has been sent, it marks all the messages it processed as read, including those it left out of the summary. They stay in the same folder if you need to find them later. If you'd rather keep unread messages unread, ask your agent to preserve their read status and save that preference.

Choose a frequency that fits the mail. If you want it to run automatically, use the scheduling instructions.

A schedule doesn't change the skill's requirement to ask before sending, but depending on the digest, you might choose to give that permission in advance. For example, I schedule the school digest skill to run twice a week, and I give it explicit permission to email me and my partner without any other approval. Since the digest is low-stakes—it's only going to us—I consider it low risk. If the digest is wrong in some way, it's an easy low-cost fix. For other types of email digests going to a larger audience, you might want to review the result before it sends. In general, I let the agent send email digests that go straight back to me automatically. Anything else, I review before sending.

Keep correcting the rules as you use it. “Include schedule changes even when they're buried in a newsletter” is an instruction the agent can use next time. Have it save that instruction, then check the next digest to see whether it followed it.

docs.title: Refresh your dashboard and project description
docs.text:
Project management skills are being updated

We’re updating the weekly-review skill to work with the project description and dashboard described on this site. You can use the prompts below now; the reusable skill is being refreshed.

After a meeting, I want a current account of what we agreed to do. What's on my plate, what's on my collaborators' plates, and am I the bottleneck for anything? Then, before the next meeting, I want to read that same dashboard and arrive with the right strategic agenda.

I use /weekly-review to keep this cycle going across all my projects. It reads the comments I've left in the Google Doc and the meeting transcript, updates the dashboard, and suggests changes to the underlying project description. That keeps the account we use for proposals and reports in step with the work we're actually doing.

The setup page explains the two tabs: Tab 1 is the dashboard and meeting log, and Tab 2 is the project description. In my research projects, I name them Overview and Research Design. I use “research design” below, but the same approach works for other project plans. The first tab should change after each meeting. The second takes more thought, since it explains what we're doing and why.

If you haven't read the build guide, you should at least start with step 5, Put both documents to work, for context on how I use both tabs.

A dashboard refresh and a meeting follow-up do different jobs. /weekly-review keeps the continuing project record current. /post-meeting prepares an account of one meeting and can draft an email about it. You don't need both after every meeting. If you just want to update the dashboard, use the transcript directly.

docs.title: 1. During the meeting, give the agent updates
docs.text:
One reason I like Google Docs is that I can leave comments while we're meeting. I tell the agent what's been handled, what the next open question is, or which table or statistic I want to see at the next meeting. Put the comment beside the relevant item so it has the context.

These comments give the agent my corrections and priorities to use in the next refresh. Leaving a comment doesn't itself run the agent. It reads them when I ask it to update the document, or when the scheduled review runs.

docs.title: 2. After the meeting, refresh the dashboard
docs.text:
After the meeting, ask the agent to:

  1. Refresh the dashboard using the comments you left in the Doc.
  2. Update it using the meeting transcript.
  3. Suggest changes to the research design based on the decisions and discussions from the meeting.

You can ask for all three in plain language:

Read my comments in the dashboard and today's meeting transcript. Use both to update Tab 1.

Then suggest any changes we should make to Tab 2 based on our decisions and discussions. I want to review those suggestions before you change the design document.

I do all three with /weekly-review, which I automate to run after the meeting. For example, one of my projects meets every Friday morning, so I run the review automatically every Friday at noon.

docs.title: 3. Install /weekly-review
docs.text:
The /weekly-review skill brings the new material together and updates the project record. You can run it after any meeting. Installing it doesn't create a recurring task. We'll set that up separately below.

Need to install the skill?

Ask your agent:

Find and install the weekly-review skill from the claudeblattman GitHub repository. Install the entire folder, containing any references, templates, and the SKILL.md file. Put it where I store all my other skills.

There are three ways to run it:

  • /weekly-review updates the dashboard and meeting history, saves the review record, and suggests changes to the research design for you to review. This is the ordinary workflow.
  • /weekly-review nosave does the same review and can still update the Google Doc, but skips the local summary file. It still keeps the records needed to check the update and avoid repeating it.
  • /weekly-review nochange shows the proposed dashboard, meeting history, and design changes in the chat without changing or saving anything.

docs.title: What the review reads
docs.text:
The review starts with the existing dashboard, your comments, and the research design. Then it looks for what's happened since the last successful review. On a first run, it uses the past week unless you ask for a different period.

The sources depend on what you've connected and saved in the project's configuration:

  • Meeting transcripts. It reads the project's saved transcripts or retrieves them from the selected Granola meetings. In my own setup, a helper fetches new transcripts from the project's Granola folder and files them locally, usually under 10_AI_Collaboration/Transcripts/. Once the review is finished, processed transcripts move into archive/ inside that folder. They remain available to read later. The public skill leaves source transcripts in place and doesn't include that filing and archiving helper. To set up local transcript filing, follow the transcript guide.
  • Email. With email connected, it uses the saved collaborator addresses and project keywords to find relevant messages to and from the team during the review period. A weekly run normally covers the past week. An email from a collaborator about a different project doesn't belong in this review.
  • Other project material. It reads the sources you've included, such as a revised proposal, working paper, shared notes, or messages from a project WhatsApp group if your agent has access. It also checks the previous dashboard snapshot, when available, to see what you've corrected directly.

These locations and search details belong in the saved project configuration. PROJECT_INDEX.md supplies links when the configuration is missing something. You shouldn't have to explain where everything lives each week. If the agent can't read a source, it should tell you.

docs.title: 4. Tell it which project to review
docs.text:
You should be able to name the project and let the agent find the right documents. It first looks for the project's configuration: the saved directions to the dashboard, the design document, and the sources it should read. If those directions are complete, it can go straight to work. Otherwise, it checks PROJECT_INDEX.md for the missing links. It asks you when it still can't find what it needs or finds conflicting destinations.

If you used /setup-project-management to set up the dashboard, the agent prepares this configuration for you. You don't need to write JSON or look up document IDs yourself. New setups use PROJECT_CONFIG.json. If that doesn't work or you don't have one, giving /weekly-review the link to your Google Doc usually does the trick. Or ask your agent to find the document in your Drive for you.

The agent should reuse the sources recorded during setup and ask only for what's missing. If you add a new source later, have it save that location for future reviews.

Check that your agent can read the Doc's comments as well as its text. If it can't, ask it to help you get that connection set up. Being able to leave a comment where you're already working is what makes this easy to keep doing.

docs.title: 5. Run the review
docs.text:
Once the project is set up and you've given the agent permission to update the dashboard, just name it:

/weekly-review Gang entry project

The review produces:

  1. The updated Tab 1 dashboard.
  2. A dated entry in the meeting history.
  3. Suggested Tab 2 changes, with the reasons and sources behind them.

Look over the result and correct anything it misunderstood. For example: “We discussed postponing this, but we didn't decide to. Keep the original deadline.” An outstanding task should stay on the dashboard until it's completed or you've decided to drop it, even if nobody mentioned it this week.

The agent should preserve your notes and earlier history, check the result, and then record the successful refresh.

Glance at Tab 1 afterward to see what you need to do. Read it more thoroughly before the next meeting to decide what deserves the team's attention. You can also use it with the project description to prepare a meeting brief.

docs.title: 6. Work through the suggested design changes
docs.text:
Every review compares the new discussions and decisions with Tab 2. For each suggested edit, the agent should show what the design currently says, the proposed replacement or addition, and the dated source behind it. It should also distinguish something we agreed from an idea we only discussed.

If it finds no supported changes, or couldn't read the design or an essential source, it should say so.

Review the specific suggestions before the agent edits Tab 2. Permission to update the dashboard, including on a schedule, doesn't give it permission to rewrite the design. You don't need to rewrite the design every time. For an established project, I'd revisit it roughly every six months, or before a new proposal. For a nascent project, every other week may make more sense. Or a substantial change in direction is a reason to spend time on it.

The review has already done the comparison. Start with its suggestions and work through the choices that need your judgment. The bulk of the thinking here belongs to you and your collaborators. Treat this as a chance to revisit the project strategically. Rewrite the parts that no longer explain what you're doing, and give the agent your decisions.

Once you've agreed on the changes, ask:

Update Tab 2 with the specific changes we've agreed on.

When you're done revising Tab 2, make any necessary changes to Tab 1 to reflect the new decisions.

Once Tab 2 reflects those decisions, use it as the starting point for the next proposal, report, or IRB application. You should be able to spend your time on what that document needs, rather than reconstructing the project again.

docs.title: 7. Schedule it for after your meeting
docs.text:
Once the review works, schedule it for after your recurring meeting. You have two options:

  • Set it up in the app. Open the scheduled-tasks section and create a recurring task with the project name, /weekly-review, and the time you want it to run. See the scheduling instructions for Codex or Claude.
  • Ask your agent to set it up. Give it the project, day, time, and timezone, as in the prompt below.

Either way, the task should appear in your app's scheduled-tasks section, where you can check or change it.

Schedule /weekly-review for [project name] every Friday at noon in [timezone].

The skill supplies the instructions. Your app or another scheduler runs them, using a document connection that can read the comments and update the right tab. Try the first automatic write in a copy of the Doc, including a correction you've made yourself, before letting it update the shared one.

Check the first scheduled result. It should tell you what you need to do after this meeting and give you a useful starting point for the next one.

docs.title: Stay on top of your health & fitness
docs.text:
This is a detailed example of Organize your projects.

This isn't a planning folder like vacation or shopping. It's a research and consultation folder. I keep a detailed markdown file with my health baseline, labs, medications, and training patterns. When I have a question — blood pressure trends, a sports injury, nutrition claims, physical therapy options — the AI gives advice that accounts for my full context instead of starting from scratch.

How I actually use this

I use this folder in a few different modes:

  • Deep thinking sessions — extended conversations where I work through a specific health question. Understanding a lab result trend, evaluating treatment options for an injury, figuring out how to modify training around a constraint.
  • Deep research reports — when I want to understand claims about nutrition, blood pressure management, or physical therapy approaches. I ask for evidence with primary sources. I'm comfortable reading the actual studies, so I ask the AI to be skeptical of small-sample or non-experimental research.
  • Quick consultations — minor ailments, aches and pains, equipment recommendations, whether a new monitoring device would be useful.

Dr. Claude and Dr. ChatGPT are both genuinely good at this. I generally trust ChatGPT most for deep research in this domain — its web browsing lets it pull current studies and reviews. Claude tends to be better for structured analysis when I already have the information.

The key insight: none of this works well without the profile file. Without it, you get generic advice for a generic person. With it, you get advice calibrated to your age, your medications, your injury history, and your actual training goals.

docs.title: What Goes in the Profile
docs.text: The canonical file is a single markdown document with your stable health context. Here's the structure — what sections to include and why each one matters.

docs.title: 1. Core baseline (table)
docs.text: A small table of stable facts: age range, height, weight range, blood pressure trend, key lab categories. Use ranges rather than exact numbers — they're more stable and more private. The AI needs "blood pressure elevated, trending down on current medication" — not your reading from last Tuesday.

docs.title: 2. Medications & supplements (table)
docs.text:
This is the most important section for safety. Columns: drug category, schedule, indication, and notes. When you ask about a new supplement, exercise protocol, or dietary change, the AI cross-references your medication list and flags interactions. Without it, you get advice that ignores contraindications.

Include notes on recent changes ("dose recently increased," "discontinued after targets met") — these give the AI context for why your current regimen looks the way it does.

docs.title: 3. Medical history & injuries (bullets)
docs.text: Chronic conditions, injury limitations, and red flags requiring clinician involvement. Write injuries in functional terms ("avoid high-impact on left knee" or "no deep flexion beyond 90°") rather than diagnostic terms. The AI needs to know what movements to modify, not your full medical chart.

docs.title: 4. Lifestyle & activity pattern (table)
docs.text: Your actual training: modalities, frequency, typical sessions, and goals. This tells the AI your real training load, so recommendations account for recovery, volume, and competing demands. If you climb three times a week and run twice, a recommendation to "add three days of HIIT" is bad advice — the AI catches that when it knows your schedule.

docs.title: 5. Family history
docs.text: Relevant family health patterns, especially anything that shapes your preventive focus. A family history of cardiac events in the 50s-60s changes every recommendation about exercise intensity, monitoring, and medication decisions.

docs.title: 6. Monitoring & devices (bullets)
docs.text: What you currently track and what tools you have. This prevents the AI from recommending "check your HRV trends" when you don't own a device that tracks HRV. Also note what you're open to adopting — the AI can make targeted suggestions.

docs.title: 7. Preferences & constraints
docs.text: How you want the AI to behave: evidence standard, tone, what to emphasize (performance vs. weight loss), what to avoid (generic tips, product upselling). If you're comfortable reading primary research, say so — it changes the depth and citation style of every response.

docs.title: 8. Update policy
docs.text: When to refresh each section: labs after each checkup, meds immediately on change, training goals quarterly. Without this, you'll be getting advice based on stale information and won't notice.

docs.title: The Instructions File
docs.text:
Separate from the profile, the project instructions tell the AI how to behave:

# Health & Fitness — Project Instructions

## Standing preferences
- Base guidance on evidence and cite primary sources
- Be skeptical of small-sample or non-experimental research
- Flag anything requiring clinician approval (lab trends,
  medication changes, etc.)
- Focus on performance and injury prevention, not generic
  weight-loss tips
- Neutral tone; avoid excessive enthusiasm

## How to use the profile
- Load or reference the master health profile at the start of
  any health- or fitness-related thread
- If information seems out of date, ask before guessing
- If a test, reading, or monitoring device would help answer
  a question, suggest it

## Privacy
- No full identifiers in outputs
- Keep advice general enough to be safe if seen by others

docs.title: When to Use Files vs. Instructions Only
docs.text:
This is a domain where uploaded files matter. Your health profile has tables of data — baseline vitals, medication lists, training patterns — that are too detailed for the instructions field alone. Upload the profile as a source file (ChatGPT) or project knowledge (Claude.ai), and keep the behavioral rules in instructions.

Compare this to shopping, where the instructions file alone is enough. The rule of thumb: if you have tables of data the AI needs to reference, upload a file. If you have rules and preferences, instructions are sufficient.

docs.title: Building Your Own Health Profile
docs.text:
Use the context-building approach from the main guide:

  1. Narrate your situation — dump your health context: conditions, medications, training, goals, injuries, what's worked and what hasn't
  2. Let the AI interview you — it will ask about medication interactions, training constraints, monitoring tools, recovery patterns, family history
  3. Generate the canonical file — have the AI synthesize it into the table structure described above

Privacy note: Be thoughtful about what goes in the file versus what you share only in conversation. The profile should contain enough for individualized advice without being a complete medical record. Use ranges instead of exact values. Keep detailed lab results in conversation, not in the permanent file.

Iteration: Your first version will be thin. After a few consultations you'll notice what's missing — usually injury constraints, medication interaction notes, or training details the AI needed but didn't have. Add those. By the fifth or sixth session, the file stabilizes and updates become a line or two after each doctor's visit or training shift.

docs.title: Build a personal shopper
docs.text:
This is a detailed example of Organize your projects.

I built my first shopping file after the third time I asked ChatGPT for a product recommendation and got a wall of options with no clear winner. The AI kept recommending unknown brands, inventing prices, and ignoring that I care more about durability than saving $20. Once I wrote down how I actually decide — and told the AI to stop guessing — the recommendations got dramatically better.

The full story: how ad hoc prompting became a system

It started the way it starts for everyone. I needed something — a piece of gear, a household item — and asked the AI "what should I buy?" I'd paste a link, maybe mention a budget. The output was inconsistent: too many options, vague tradeoffs, and confident claims about prices and availability that turned out to be wrong.

The first failure mode I noticed: it didn't remember that I value durability over marginal savings. Every new conversation, I'd re-explain my decision style from scratch. The second: it would recommend 15 options when I needed 3. The third: it sounded certain about things it couldn't possibly know — stock levels, sale prices, review consensus.

So I started adding rules. No hallucinated specs. Label uncertainty explicitly. Shortlist only — 3 to 5 picks, not 15. Explain tradeoffs and failure modes. That made outputs more reliable, but still generic.

The real shift came when I separated how I decide from what I'm buying now. My decision criteria — durability, return policy, total cost of ownership, established brands over unknowns — don't change between purchases. So I pulled them into a canonical file. The per-purchase details (budget, timeline, use case) go into a brief I paste fresh each time.

After about five purchases, the file stabilized. I wasn't rewriting it — just adding a line after each buy. "Check parts availability for anything with a motor." "Discount 'just arrived' reviews." The system got better without getting bigger.

docs.title: Anatomy of a Real Shopping File
docs.text:
Unlike the vacation example, where I upload reference files as sources, shopping needs only an instructions file. The decision criteria and behavioral rules fit in a few paragraphs — no tables of data required.

Here's the structure of my actual shopping instructions, with annotations explaining why each section exists.

docs.title: Decision posture
docs.text:
- Prioritize best-in-class or best value-for-money products.
  Mention budget options when durability is less critical. # (1)
- Avoid unknown or low-quality brands, especially random
  marketplace imports. Favor well-known, trusted brands. # (2)
- Value durability and long-term satisfaction over first
  impressions. Highlight reviews reflecting long-term use. # (3)
  1. Why "best-in-class or best value": Without this, the AI optimizes for price — which is the wrong objective for most purchases. This one line reframes every recommendation.
  2. Why "avoid unknown brands": AI chatbots love recommending cheap imports with inflated reviews. This forces it to default to established brands unless you explicitly opt in to risk.
  3. Why "long-term satisfaction": Most positive reviews are written in the first week. The AI needs to weight long-term ownership reports and failure-mode descriptions, not "just arrived" praise.

docs.title: How to recommend
docs.text:
- Provide curated shortlists (3-5 picks), side-by-side
  comparisons, and pros/cons summaries.
- Include links to expert reviews (e.g., Wirecutter, Outdoor
  Gear Lab). I like to read the deep dives myself. # (1)
- Do not recommend subscription or auto-renewal options
  unless explicitly requested. # (2)
  1. Why "include expert review links": The AI's own product knowledge is unreliable for specific models and prices. Pointing to trusted review sources gives you something to verify against.
  2. Why "no subscriptions": Left to its own devices, the AI will recommend subscription services for everything. This prevents it from optimizing for recurring revenue that doesn't serve you.

docs.title: Buying logistics
docs.text:
- Default to online shopping. Preferred retailers: Amazon Prime,
  plus trusted specialty retailers with strong reputations. # (1)
- Factor in delivery costs — free or low-cost shipping preferred.
- Alert me if a relevant sale period is approaching (Prime Day,
  Black Friday, seasonal sales for relevant categories). # (2)
  1. Why specify retailers: This prevents recommendations from sketchy marketplaces with bad return policies. The AI will find the cheapest source unless you tell it to factor in the buying experience.
  2. Why sale alerts: Simple but easy to forget. The AI knows seasonal patterns — if you're buying outdoor gear in May, it should flag that REI's anniversary sale is coming.

docs.title: Durability and context
docs.text:
- Strong warranties are a plus for outdoor and activity gear.
  For everyday goods, durability matters more than warranty.
- Family with kids — sometimes shopping for children, including
  short-term-use items where lower cost is acceptable. # (1)
- [Your ecosystem: e.g., Apple devices, specific audio system,
  PC for a family member. Smart home details if relevant.]
- [Your interests: e.g., outdoor sports, cooking, reading,
  travel. These shape gear and gift recommendations.]
  1. Why "kids" as a modifier: Without this, the AI applies adult durability standards to everything. Kids' items often have a 6-month useful life — the calculus is different, and the AI needs to know that.

docs.title: Step 1: Paste a run brief
docs.text:
Each purchase gets a short brief — what you're buying, the use case, must-haves, budget, and timeline. Here's what one looks like:

Item: Standing desk for home office
Use case: Daily use, 8+ hours. Need to alternate sitting/standing.

Must-haves:
- Stable at standing height (no wobble during typing)
- Fits 2 monitors + laptop
- Quiet motor

Nice-to-haves:
- Memory presets for sitting/standing heights
- Cable management built in

Constraints:
- Budget: under $700
- Width: max 60 inches (alcove)
- Timeline: no rush, can wait for a sale
- Buying channel: online with easy returns

Avoid: particle board tops, brands I can't find long-term reviews for

Notice what's not in the brief: how I evaluate products, my review-reading heuristics, my preference for durability over price. All of that lives in the instructions file. The brief is just the situation-specific layer.

docs.title: Step 2: Review the structured output
docs.text:
The AI produces a consistent format every time:

  1. Shortlist — 3-5 picks, labeled (best overall, best value, best upgrade)
  2. Comparison table — small, scannable
  3. Who each pick is for — one line each
  4. Failure modes — what commonly goes wrong and what to check before buying
  5. Buy path — where to buy, return/warranty notes, counterfeit risk
  6. Questions — only if truly needed, max 5

This structure isn't decorative — it prevents the AI from producing walls of unstructured text that require you to do the analysis yourself.

docs.title: Step 3: Close the loop
docs.text:
After you buy (and especially after you've used the product), do a 2-minute debrief. The AI proposes a canonical update — 0 to 5 stable learnings, each mapped to a specific section of your instructions file.

The decision rule: Would this learning change my recommendation for a future, different purchase? If yes, add it. If it's specific to this one product, skip it.

Field note

After buying outdoor gear, I learned that "check parts availability" matters more than brand reputation for anything with replaceable components. That one line — added after a single purchase — improved every gear recommendation afterward.

docs.text:

Compare them against my evaluation criteria.
Include a comparison table and recommend one, with the key
tradeoff that would make you switch your recommendation.

docs.title: Replacement / upgrade
docs.text:
Replacing: [current product and what's wrong with it]

docs.title: Common Failure Modes (and the Fixes)
docs.text:
The guardrails in the instructions file aren't arbitrary. Each one exists because of a specific failure:

Failure What happens Fix in the file Too many options 15 picks, no clear winner Shortlist cap (3-5) + forced tradeoffs Junk brands Unknown imports with inflated reviews Default to reputable; require opt-in for risk Spec-sheet bait Feature lists instead of real-world fit Emphasize failure modes, warranty, long-term reviews Invented facts Confident prices, stock levels, review claims "Unknown unless provided"; label uncertainty Ignored constraints Recommends something that doesn't fit Run brief requires constraints; AI must check them File bloat Instructions become a junk drawer Stable-only rule + size limit + quarterly prune

docs.title: Get help planning a vacation, from ideation to logistics
docs.text:
This is a detailed example of Organize your projects.

The first file I built wasn't for research. It was for planning family vacations. That sounds trivial, but it taught me the pattern I now use for everything — shopping, health, finances, even rock climbing trip logistics. We once planned a trip to a great spot for climbing and rafting. Turned out it was one of the hotter times of year — we lost several outdoor days. That failure is what taught me to add explicit temperature thresholds instead of vague preferences like "we don't like heat."

The full story: how a messy dump became a system

It started as a brain dump. My wife and I were planning a summer trip and I pasted a wall of text into ChatGPT — where we'd been, what the kids liked, what we couldn't stand. The AI gave decent suggestions but kept recommending beach resorts, which isn't us.

So I refined the dump. Added explicit "avoids" for each family member. Added temperature thresholds instead of "we prefer mild weather." Added past trip patterns — not just where we went, but which conditions made them work: high altitude, desert-like, culturally rich small towns.

By the third or fourth trip planned this way, the file had stabilized. I wasn't rewriting it anymore — just adding a line or two after each trip. "This destination worked when we had a car but would fail without one." "That region is too hot in July despite being great in October."

After about six conversations, the file was reliable enough to trust. New trip planning conversations started producing useful, specific suggestions on the first exchange. No warm-up. No re-explaining who we are. The AI already knew we're a family of four with a teen who rides horses, a tween who lives for adventure sports, a parent who rock climbs, and another who wants natural beauty and water activities — and that all of us hate crowded tourist traps.

That's when I realized: this isn't a vacation hack. It's a pattern. Any recurring task where you have stable preferences and learn from past experience can work this way. Shopping. Health decisions. Professional writing. Finances. The domain changes. The structure doesn't.

docs.title: Anatomy of a Real Project: Vacation Planning
docs.text: Here's the structure of my actual vacation planning file, with annotations explaining why each section exists.

docs.title: System instructions
docs.text:
I want you to be an unusually investigative advisor for travel. # (1)
Instead of focusing on being highly agreeable, be analytical and
offer critical opinions where appropriate. # (2)

When starting a new discussion, analyze the prompt and come back with:
* What kind of vacation we want (outdoorsy, urban, cultural, etc.)
* Who is going (if not clear)
* Major red flags based on my preferences # (3)
* Potential travel restrictions (visa, vaccination, safety warnings)

Please do not hallucinate details but investigate and confirm
wherever possible. # (4)

Provide 1.5 to 2 times more activity options than we have time
available so that we can pick and choose.
  1. Why "unusually investigative": Without this, the AI defaults to agreeable mode — it recommends whatever you seem excited about. You want it to push back and surface problems early.
  2. Why "not agreeable": Left to its own devices, the AI will cheerfully recommend a destination that violates three of your constraints. This instruction makes it flag conflicts instead of burying them.
  3. Why "major red flags": This is the constraint-checking instruction. It forces the AI to cross-reference your preferences before generating suggestions, not after.
  4. Why "do not hallucinate": AI chatbots will confidently invent hotel prices, restaurant hours, and activity availability. This instruction doesn't eliminate hallucination, but it reduces confident fabrication and encourages the AI to flag uncertainty.

docs.title: Persona preferences
docs.text:
Each family member gets their own section with preferences AND avoids. Here's one:

### Teen Daughter
- Passions: Animals (especially horses — horseback riding is her top priority),
  water sports, reading, bookstores, shopping
- Adventure: Thrill rides, water parks, river rafting, swimming
- Avoids: Steady uphill hikes (unless scrambly or leading to water),
  heavy insect areas, long drives without stops
- Shopping: Loves used bookstores with good YA/fantasy sections,
  boutique clothing stores

The design pattern: preferences tell the AI what to suggest. Avoids tell it what to filter out. Without the avoids, you'll get recommendations that technically match the preferences but fail in practice.

docs.title: Logistics constraints
docs.text:
## Climate & Weather Requirements
- Temperature: Prefer daytime highs 65-80°F; flag anything over 85°F
- Humidity: Low humidity preferred, especially if over 80°F
- Rain: Highlight wet seasons or inclement periods

## Travel Logistics
- Base strategy: Prefer one home base for 5-7 days with activities
  within 75-minute drives, rather than constant destination changes
- Driving limits: Maximum 8 hours/day, preferably 4
- Accommodation: Heavy users of home exchange; destination choice
  often driven by available exchanges
- Crowds: Avoid extremely touristy places; favor off-season or
  weekdays when possible

Every constraint has a number. Not "we don't like long drives" but "maximum 8 hours, preferably 4." Not "mild weather" but "65-80°F, flag over 85°F."

docs.title: Evidence bank
docs.text:
## Successful Past Patterns
- Mountain/high altitude — Pacific Northwest in summer (worked: climate,
  outdoor sports, uncrowded)
- Cultural/authentic — Southern Mexico (worked: food scene, local flavor,
  affordable, kids engaged)
- Desert/semi-arid — Desert Southwest in winter (worked: climbing, mild
  temps, unique landscape)

## Good but Imperfect
- Coastal Mexico resort town (too muggy; inland towns were better)
- Pacific Northwest river town (fewer activities than expected;
  worked when we had water sports gear)
- Major European cities in summer (too crowded; rural areas
  in the same countries were excellent)

Tag each entry with its conditions. "Worked when we had a car." "Failed in summer heat." This is the most powerful section of the file — it gives the AI pattern-matching data instead of just preference lists.

docs.title: Step 1: Start a new conversation
docs.text: Open a new thread in the project. Paste a short trip brief alongside the canonical file (or let the project instructions load automatically). The brief is situation-specific: dates, who's going, any special constraints for this particular trip.

docs.title: Step 2: Review the AI's initial response
docs.text:
The AI may ask clarifying questions first, or it may dive straight into suggestions. Both are normal. Before engaging with the suggestions, check: did it reference your constraints? Did it flag anything from your avoids? If it's giving generic output, reprompt: "Reference my project file. Which of my stated constraints does each option satisfy or violate?"

Field note

My first version got Top 10 tourist lists. Adding explicit "avoids" per person changed everything. The AI went from suggesting beach resorts (which we rarely enjoy) to suggesting mountain towns and cultural small cities — exactly our pattern.

docs.title: Step 3: Compare options with explicit trade-offs
docs.text:
Ask the AI to generate 1.5-2x the options you need, with explicit trade-offs for each. A good response looks like: "Option A is best for the climber and worst for the teen. Option B satisfies everyone at a 7/10 but nobody at a 10/10. Option C is ideal weather but a 9-hour drive."

Field note

The biggest upgrade: past trip patterns as evidence. Instead of "we like mild weather," I wrote "trips that worked: high altitude, desert, culturally rich small cities." It immediately stopped suggesting beach resorts.

docs.title: Step 4: Narrow and build the itinerary
docs.text: Pick 1-2 top options. Ask for a realistic itinerary with pacing discipline — not a packed schedule that ignores your stated preference for late mornings or your kids' energy limits.

docs.title: Step 5: After the trip, update the file
docs.text:
Add 1-2 stable learnings. Not an essay — one new rule, one updated threshold.

The decision rule: "Would this change my recommendation for the next trip, even to a different destination? If yes, add it to the file. If it's specific to this trip's conditions, skip it."

Field note

We planned a trip to a region known for climbing and rafting. Turned out it was one of the hotter times of year — limited our climbing days significantly. That's when I added explicit temperature thresholds: "flag anything over 85°F." Two words of specificity prevented the same mistake from recurring.

docs.title: Example Trip Brief
docs.text:
Here's an actual brief I've used (sanitized), showing how little context you need when the canonical file is doing its job:

Planning: 10 days, late July. Full family (4 people).

Region: Pacific Northwest — interested in a mountain town near
major climbing areas.

Must-haves:
- Multi-pitch rock climbing accessible within 45 min of base
- Horseback riding options for the teen
- River or lake activities (SUP, kayak, rafting)
- Good restaurant/brewery scene in the town itself

Watch for:
- Heat management — check historical highs for late July
- Wildfire smoke risk in this region/season
- Book popular activities 2+ weeks ahead (horse riding, guided rafting)

Open question: Is it worth splitting the trip — 6 days mountain town
+ 4 days at the coast? Or better to commit to one base?

Notice what's not in the brief: family preferences, budget philosophy, accommodation style, driving limits, crowd preferences. All of that lives in the canonical file. The brief is just the situation-specific layer.

Other brief styles I use:

  • Comparison / decision problem: "We're choosing between two coastal cities. Please compare them across our criteria and recommend one. Include a comparison table." — useful when you're stuck between options.
  • Exploratory / feasibility check: "My son and I want a father-son trip focused on soccer and Spanish immersion in Latin America. Is this realistic for a 10-day window? What are the best options?" — useful when you're not sure the idea even works.

docs.title: Copy-ready brief templates
docs.text:
Use these as starting points for different planning modes:

Two-destination routing:

Planning: [DURATION], [DATES]. [WHO IS GOING].

Route: [DESTINATION A] → [DESTINATION B]
Split: [X] days at A, [Y] days at B, [Z] day transit

Destination A priorities:
- [Activity/goal 1]
- [Activity/goal 2]

Destination B priorities:
- [Activity/goal 1]
- [Activity/goal 2]

Transit day: Recommend a worthwhile stop between A and B?
Open question: [Your actual uncertainty about this trip]

Single base + day trips:

Planning: [DURATION], [DATES]. [WHO IS GOING].

Base: [TOWN/REGION]
Radius: Day trips within [X] minutes drive

Must-do activities:
- [Activity 1]
- [Activity 2]

Day trip ideas (rank by priority for our family):
- [Potential day trip 1]
- [Potential day trip 2]

Rain plan: If weather turns, what's the best swap from the day
trip list to an indoor/covered alternative?

Skills/activities with daily constraint:

Planning: [DURATION], [DATES]. [WHO IS GOING].

Focus: [PRIMARY ACTIVITY — e.g., climbing, diving, language school]
Daily constraint: [PERSON] needs [X] — build this into every day

Structure each day as modular 60-90 minute blocks:
- Morning block: [primary activity]
- Midday block: [flexible — could be rest, food, or secondary activity]
- Afternoon block: [secondary activity or family time]

Flag any days where the primary activity isn't available
(weather, closures, rest days) and suggest alternatives.

docs.title: Optional Add-Ons
docs.text:
You probably don't need these. Add them only when you feel recurring pain in one of these areas:

  • Decision matrix — When you're stuck between 3+ options and need a structured comparison. Ask the AI to build a weighted scoring table against your criteria.
  • Research log — When source quality matters. Track which recommendations were AI-generated vs. independently verified.
  • Post-trip reflection — Five bullet points: what worked, what didn't, what to add to the file, what to remove, what surprised you.
  • Packing module — Families with kids tend to adopt this first. Stable packing lists per person, per trip type, with "don't forget" flags from past experience.
  • Booking/logistics checklist — Time-sensitive tasks: what to book early, what to book late, what requires advance reservations in your typical destinations.
